parts.title: Killing plateau pikas harms grasslands, and fencing out livestock does not make them better
parts.abstract:
Summary

On the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, high in western China, the grasslands have been getting worse for years. The two main ways people have tried to fix this are killing off the plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae), a small, round, rabbit-like animal that lives in burrows, and putting up fences to keep grazing livestock out. To find out how well these methods work, we looked at 14 years of measurements from 1,460 small patches of grassland, spread across 22 different natural regions.

We used a method called structural equation modeling, which lets us trace how one change can ripple through a chain of other changes. It showed that getting rid of pikas had a weak, roundabout harmful effect on how stable the grassland was, meaning how steadily its plants kept growing from one year to the next. Neither years of pika control nor fencing led to significant overall improvements. In other words, our statistical tests could not show that either one made the grassland better as a whole.

Some grazing arrangements did help at first. They raised the number of plant species, counting both the plants livestock like to eat and the ones they don't (+18.7%). They also raised the amount of plant material from plants livestock don't like to eat (+27.4%). But these gains faded after 8–10 years, and things went back to where they started.

These findings show that killing plateau pikas without careful thought makes the grassland a worse home for wildlife and brings no lasting benefit. They also show that fencing off large areas fails to significantly increase the number of plant species or make the grassland more stable. Our results suggest that relying on just one method at a time is not the best approach. We need ways of managing grasslands that combine several methods and adjust to how nature actually works.

Subject areas: environmental science, environmental management, agricultural science
parts.introduction_first:
Scientists and the people who make government rules often pull in different directions. Scientists try to be careful and follow the evidence wherever it leads, while policymakers have to act and get things done. This clash is especially sharp when people are trying to look after nature. Living things are linked in complicated ways, and a change in one place can loop back and cause surprises somewhere else. Meanwhile, communities and economies want quick fixes.

China's vast grazing lands, which cover 4 million square kilometers, are a clear example of this problem. Since 2000, the effort to repair these grasslands has been dominated by two approaches. One is fencing out livestock, which has now been going on for more than 25 years. The other is large programs to kill plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae). These efforts have cost a great deal of money, more than 12 billion since 2010, and they now cover 78% of the damaged grasslands. Even so, scientists still argue about whether they make ecological sense and whether they can work over the long run.

New evidence points to some unexpected results. One is a break in the food chain that spreads from one kind of living thing to the next. Another is the landscape becoming more and more the same everywhere, losing its natural patchwork of different places. These surprises challenge the basic ideas behind the way grasslands are managed today.
parts.introduction_rest:
For a long time, the usual way of managing grasslands has treated plateau pikas as pests. The idea was that they compete with livestock for the plants the animals eat. This view has led to huge programs to kill off small burrowing animals. In Mongolia, controlling a related animal called Brandt's vole has cost between $300,000 and $800,000 every year.

In China, large-scale programs to kill these animals began in the 1960s. Over the years, the poisons have changed. First came zinc phosphide, then a poison called NH4+–fluoroacetate. Today the most common ones are poisons that stop blood from clotting, such as diphacinone-Na, along with botulin toxin C. According to the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture, 38,000 tons of rodent poison were used in each year from 2003 to 2005.

Newer research on how nature works paints a more complicated picture. Pikas act as "ecosystem engineers," meaning they reshape their surroundings in ways that affect many other living things. When they dig their burrows, they let more air into the soil and help nutrients move through it. The way pikas pick which plants to eat may also hold back plants that livestock don't like to eat, and under certain conditions it may help grasses and grass-like plants grow. Because pikas affect the grassland in so many ways, we need to rethink how they are managed.

Fencing out livestock is still one of the most common ways of trying to repair damaged pastures. People value it because it is cheap and can easily be used over large areas. Since 2003, a Chinese program called "returning grazing land to grassland" has put fences around 57,600 square kilometers of damaged high-mountain grassland in northern Tibet to keep livestock out. In 2011, the program grew bigger with a payment scheme. Herders now receive 90 RMB (about 12 US dollars) per hectare each year for fencing off damaged pastures. A hectare is 10,000 square meters, roughly the size of a large sports field. Even so, nobody has yet carefully checked whether this fencing actually helps the grassland.

There is still a lot we don't know about whether today's grassland repair methods work over large areas and whether their effects last. Many small studies exist, but very few look at many natural regions at once or follow them over many years. To answer these questions, we set up a long-term network for watching the grasslands. It covered 22 natural regions, which together make up 85% of China's high-mountain meadows, and we took measurements every year for 14 years, from 2005 to 2018.

We kept track of 1,460 small patches of grassland, recording exactly where each one was. We picked the patches at random, but within set groups, so that every part of the landscape was fairly covered. On average, each region had 66.3 patches.

With this network, we set out to answer three main questions. First, how does fencing off whole landscapes change the way the plant community develops over time, and what the grassland provides for people and nature? Second, does years of killing plateau pikas lead to a lasting change in the food chain, or does it just shift the problem somewhere else? Third, in grasslands that never settle into a fixed balance, how many years pass before the benefits of these management methods begin to fade?

## STAR★Methods: how we did the study

### Key resources table

This table lists the data and computer tools we used, where they came from, and where to find them.

|---|---|---|

| **Software and methods** | | |

| piecewiseSEM R package (v2.3.1) | Lefcheck38 | https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=piecewiseSEM |
| dplyr R package (v1.1.4) | Wickham et al.39 | https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dplyr |
| ggplot2 R package | Wickham40 | https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org |

R is a free computer language for statistics. ArcGIS is a program for making and studying maps. The R "packages" are add-on toolkits for R, and BioRender is a tool for drawing scientific pictures.

### The animal we studied

The animal at the center of this study is the plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae), a small mammal found only on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We did not look at whether males and females gave different results. That is because pika control was carried out on whole populations within particular natural regions, and we measured what happened to the plant communities, not to individual animals. All our field observations involving animals were done with permission from our institutions and under their oversight for animal welfare.

### Method details

#### Where we worked

Our study took place in Qinghai Province, on the northeast side of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Figure 1). This is high country: most of the land lies between 3000 and 5000 meters above sea level.41,42 The climate is harsh, with bitter winters and big swings between seasons. The average yearly temperature is below freezing. Historically it has been 0°C, and during the study period, 2005-2018, it was -0.5°C. On average, 540 mm of rain and snow falls each year, and 70% of it arrives between June and August (Figure 1).

The soils are mainly of three types: alpine meadow, scrub meadow and bog.43 On them grow the plant communities typical of the region: alpine meadows, shrublands and dry grassy plains called steppes. The most common plants are sedges (Carex spp. and Kobresia spp.), feather grasses (Stipa spp.), Achantherum splendens and the shrub Potentilla fruticose.44

#### How we set up the experiment

We compared three common ways of managing the land (Figure 1). The first was ordinary pastures grazed in winter and summer, which served as our comparison group, or "Control." The second was fencing out livestock for many years ("Fence"). The third was plateau pika control. In May 2005 we set up 62 study areas in several counties across Qinghai. Each covered more than 20 hectares, measuring 500 m by 400 m. (A hectare is a square 100 m on each side.) Each type of management was kept going steadily for cycles lasting more than 3 years (Table S1). The sites had the gently rolling land and thin plant cover typical of grazed high-mountain pastures.

We set the grazing levels to follow a Chinese farming standard for how many animals a piece of land can support, code NY/T 635-2015. Following advice from local grassland stations, every site was grazed at about 1.0 yak per hectare, with a feeding rate of 45%–55%, meaning the share of the grass the animals were expected to eat. To keep livestock out of the fenced areas, we put up permanent wire mesh fences with their bottom edge more than 15 cm above the ground. This kept out large grazing animals but still let small creatures, such as voles and other small rodents, pass underneath.

We chose 30 sites for pika control, picking places where no pika control had been done before (Table S1). Pikas were controlled across outer buffer zones larger than 20 hectares. Inside each zone, we marked out a central area of less than 5 hectares where we took our measurements. The buffer around it helped make sure the area we measured had been fully treated. The pikas were killed with a poison called botulin C, mixed into wheat bait and placed straight into their burrows.

#### Field survey

In each study area, we set up five plots, each 10 m by 10 m, placed at random and at least 50 m apart. Every plot sat more than 20 m in from the edge of the site. Conditions near a boundary can differ from those farther inside, so this kept that "edge effect" from affecting our results. Inside each plot, we randomly placed three parallel squares measuring 1 m by 1 m, called quadrats, and sampled the plants in them (Table S2).

We sorted the plants into three groups based on what local livestock, especially yaks, prefer to eat. These groups were plants livestock like to eat, plants livestock don't like to eat, and plants livestock avoid. To make this grouping, we used regional guides to the local plants and talked with local herders about which plants their yaks eat.45,46 For each 10 m by 10 m plot, we worked out the plant community measurements by averaging the results from its three quadrats.

To measure the amount of plant material, we cut all the plants in each quadrat at ground level. We then dried them in an oven at 65 °C for 48 hours, until their weight stopped changing, which shows all the water had gone. We weighed the dried plants on a precise scale that measures to the nearest 0.1 g. We did this survey every year in late July, when the plants are at their fullest growth of the season. This way, the amount of plant material could be compared fairly from one year to the next.

### How we measured and analyzed the results

#### Calculating the grassland measures

We counted the number of plant species as the total number of different kinds of plants found in each 1 m by 1 m quadrat.

To show how stable the grassland was, we used a measure called the Inverse Coefficient of Variation (ICV).47 It compares how much plant material a spot usually has with how much that amount jumps around from year to year:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here, μ is the average amount of plant material above ground across the years of the experiment. σ is the standard deviation of that amount over time. The standard deviation is a number that shows how far the yearly values typically wander from the average. So a high ICV means plenty of plant material that stays fairly steady from year to year, which is what we mean by a stable grassland.

#### Statistical analysis

We did our statistical work in R (version 4.3.0). Our main tool was a type of model called a linear mixed-effects model, built with the 'lmer' function from the 'lme4' package (version 1.1.33). We used these models to measure how climate and land management affected three things: the number of plant species, how stable the grassland was, and the amount of plant material. We looked at each of these separately for the three groups of plants: those livestock avoid, those they don't like to eat, and those they like to eat.

A mixed-effects model sorts the possible influences into two kinds. The first kind, called fixed effects, are the influences we actually wanted to measure. Ours were the type of management (control, fencing or plateau pika control), the climate (the average yearly temperature and the yearly rain and snow), and their interactions. An interaction asks whether the effect of one factor changes depending on another, for example whether fencing works differently in wetter years. The second kind, called a random effect, handles background differences we wanted to allow for but not study. We treated "county" this way, because sites in the same county may share local conditions.

Every model used a total of 1,460 observations. These add up all the yearly measurements taken across all the study plots over the whole experiment. In the results from these models, we mark statistically significant findings with asterisks (∗∗∗), standing for p < 0.05. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

In our graphs, the summary plots show the average plus or minus the standard error of the mean. The standard error shows roughly how precisely we have pinned down the average. The graphs of changes over time also show 95% confidence intervals, a shaded range that shows how uncertain each estimate is.

To understand what drives changes in how stable the grassland is, we used structural equation modeling. We ran it with the 'psem' function from the 'piecewiseSEM' package (version 2.3.0). We used the 'dplyr' package (version 1.1.2) to organize the data.48 Most of our pictures and diagrams were made with BioRender.com.
parts.results:
## Results

### How the repair methods changed the grasslands

In the areas where plateau pikas were killed off, the number of plant species went up clearly. This was true for all plants taken together, for the plants livestock like to eat, and for the plants livestock actively avoid. Each rise was statistically significant (p < 0.05). This means that if pika control really made no difference, a gap this large would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time. Our effect estimates, which measure the size of each change compared with the ordinary grazed areas we used for comparison (the "control" areas), ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 (Figures 1 and 2). Pika control also raised the amount of plant material from plants livestock avoid, with an effect estimate of 1.85 (Figure 2).

Fencing out livestock told a different story. We found no differences between fenced and grazed areas in the number of plant species, whether we looked at all plants, plants livestock avoid, plants they don't like to eat, or plants they like to eat. In the same way, fencing did not change how stable the grassland was, or the amount of plant material, for any of these four groups when compared with the grazed areas.

**Figure 1. Where we studied, and what the sites were like, in Qinghai Province**

(A) Box charts show the average yearly temperature (MAT) and average yearly rain and snow (MAP) at the study sites from 2005 to 2018. Each box shows the middle value (the median) and the range covering the middle half of the sites (the interquartile range, or IQR). The lines sticking out of each box reach up to 1.5 times the IQR.

(B) Maps show where the study patches lie across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

(C) Photos taken in the field show the three ways the land was managed: grazing (the control), plateau pika control (PC), and fencing out livestock (fence).

**Figure 2. How the repair methods affected the number of plant species, how stable the grassland was, and the amount of plant material above the ground (AGB)**

Values are averages, with bars showing the standard error of the mean (SEM), a measure of how precisely each average is known (n = 1,460 observations). PC: plateau pika control; fence: fencing out livestock. Asterisks (∗∗∗) mark results that were statistically significant at p < 0.05, using linear mixed-effects models, a kind of statistical model that allows for the fact that repeated measurements from the same place are linked. Images were made with BioRender.com.

To see how plant communities responded up close, we looked in detail at two typical patches. In the fenced patch (called Banma96), grass-like plants such as *Poa annua* and *Elymas nutons* were the most common (Table S1). There, both the number of plant species and the amount of plant material stayed steady from year to year, for every group of plants, whether livestock liked them or not (Figure S2).

In the patch where pikas were killed off (called Gande85), plants livestock avoid made up between 6.25% and 23.53% of all the plants growing there. The most common of these was *Oxytropis ochrocephala* Bunge. In this patch, both the number of species and the amount of plant material from plants livestock avoid showed a statistically significant upward trend over time (Figure S2). The total abundance of plant species also grew more in the pika-control patch, by 31.25%, than in the fenced patch, where it grew by 6.25% (Table S3).

Across the whole region, grasslands that had been fenced for many years ended up in about the same overall condition as the grazed ones (see Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). But when we looked site by site, the picture was mixed. Out of 32 sites, fencing raised the total amount of plant material at 14 sites and lowered it at the other 18, and both kinds of change were statistically significant (p < 0.05). The number of plant species rose at 13 sites and fell at 19, again with statistically significant changes (p < 0.05). How stable the grassland was did not change at any site compared with the grazed areas, and none of these differences were significant (p > 0.05) (Table S6). So, although fencing out livestock for a long time made little difference across the region as a whole, its effects varied a great deal from one place to another.

### How pika control affected grassland stability in a roundabout way

We found that grasslands were more stable where there was less plant material from plants livestock avoid (a path strength of −0.23) and more species of plants livestock don't like to eat (a path strength of −0.20) (Figure 3). These path strengths are numbers that show how closely two things move together, on a common scale so they can be compared.

Killing off pikas had a harmful effect on grassland stability, but only in a roundabout, indirect way. It worked mainly like a chain. Pika control changed the resources available to plants, which changed the number of species of plants livestock avoid. That, in turn, changed the amount of plant material from those avoided plants, and this finally made the grassland less stable.

Our structural equation models showed a statistically significant fit to the data for explaining grassland stability (p = 0.29). Together, these models accounted for 13% of the differences in how stable the grasslands were.

**Figure 3. Structural equation modeling of how well pika control worked, based on our measurements**

Every arrow shows a statistically significant link. The number on each arrow is a standardized path strength (an "r" value). A plus or minus sign shows whether two things rise together or move in opposite directions, and ± marks a link that goes both ways (p = 0.29). The diagrams were made with BioRender.com.

### How the grasslands changed over time under each method

Between 2005 and 2018, fencing out livestock made little difference to the number of plant species or to how stable the grassland was, and these differences were not significant (p > 0.05). Pika control was different. Where pikas were killed off, the amount of plant material from plants livestock like to eat rose, and this rise was statistically significant (p < 0.05). Pika control also raised the amount of plant material from plants livestock avoid in 2011 and 2012 (p < 0.05). Overall, the grasslands under both fencing and pika control went up and down over the years rather than moving steadily in one direction (Figure 4; Table S7).

**Figure 4. How plant variety and the amount of plant material changed from 2005 to 2018 for each group of plants (all, avoided, disliked, and liked by livestock) under the three kinds of management: control (grazing), fence, and PC (plateau pika control)**

Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals, the range where the true value most likely lies.

In the grazed control areas, several measures rose in a statistically significant way over the 14 years from 2005 to 2018. These were the number of plant species overall, among plants livestock like to eat, and among plants they don't like to eat, along with the amount of plant material from plants livestock avoid. Each rise was then followed by a statistically significant fall, but the overall trend was still upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

### Grazing compared with fencing out livestock

We found that when we looked across the whole region, grassland kept fenced for many years ended up in about the same condition as grassland where livestock grazed freely. Up close, at individual sites, the picture was different: fencing led to very different results from place to place. This matters because people often take results from small fencing experiments and assume they will hold true over much larger areas. Our findings challenge that habit.

The sites did not all respond the same way. At nearly half of them, the amount of plant material went up after fencing, while at the others it went down (Table S6). This shows the limits of using one uniform plan across a landscape made up of many different kinds of places. Fencing did not simply help everywhere or harm everywhere. Instead, how well it worked seems to depend on local conditions, such as which plants grow there, what the soil is like, and how the land has been grazed in the past.

Other researchers have pointed out that drawing broad conclusions from small fencing experiments may lead to wrong predictions [21, 22]. Small studies often miss the wider setting needed to judge realistically how a management plan will work [23]. We recommend that future studies collect measurements at several scales, from small patches up to whole landscapes, so they properly capture how much places differ from one another. That approach would give more reliable advice for building conservation plans that are aimed at particular places and fit the natural variety found in grasslands.

We should also point out that most of our monitoring sites were in the southeast of Qinghai Province. The northwest is mostly empty Gobi desert. It has no grassland plants and is not suitable for grazing, so we could not collect data there. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau also has a great many small local climates, so whether our conclusions apply to other regions still needs to be checked. Future studies that cover a wider area would help test whether these patterns hold across different climate and nature zones.

### Grazing compared with killing off pikas

Pika control has been studied less than fencing or grazing, but it is carried out in many places to protect the plants livestock like to eat. Unlike grazing, pika control did not change the amount of plants livestock like to eat. Instead, it led to a clear rise in both the number of species and the amount of plant material of the plants livestock avoid. This rise was statistically significant (p < 0.05). That means that if pika control really made no difference, a gap this large would show up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

We think this can be explained by two effects that often work together in plant communities. In the first, different plants use different resources and fill in around one another. In the second, some plants do especially well under the conditions they face. Every plant has its own place and role in the community, which ecologists call its niche. Here, long years of grazing under pika control held back the plants livestock like to eat. That left their niches empty, and the plants livestock avoid moved in to take them over [24, 25] (Figure S1).

However, as the amount of these avoided plants rose, the grassland as a whole became less stable (Figure 3). So using pika control on its own may be a bad idea. It could end up harming the places where wild animals live, while doing little for farm animals.

These findings challenge the common belief that plateau pikas cause the plants livestock avoid to increase and the plants they like to decrease [26, 27, 28, 29] (see Figures 2 and 3, Figure S1 and Table S4). Our study started from the widely held assumption that pikas compete with livestock for food and help damage grazing land. The evidence, though, points to a more complicated relationship.

Plateau pikas are choosy about what they eat, and their diet does not necessarily clash with what livestock eat [30]. They mainly eat grasses and sedges (grass-like plants), but they also eat a lot of broad-leaved flowering plants, including plants from the pea family, called legumes. For example, one study looked under a microscope at plant bits in pikas' stomachs. It found that Oxytropis plants, including O. glabra and O. kansuensis, made up a large part of what pikas ate in meadows where the grass Elymus nutans was the main plant [31]. These legumes contain alkaloids and other natural chemicals that usually stop animals from eating them. Pikas, however, seem able to get around these chemicals thanks to special tiny microbes living in their guts. This lets their diet fit the unusual chemical make-up of plants in high-mountain grasslands [32].

What pikas eat also changes with the seasons. In the cold months they eat a wider variety of plants, and the plant Potentilla anserina becomes an important part of their diet then. This shows how pikas adjust their feeding as their surroundings change. In fact, when overgrazing leads to a spread of plants livestock find hard to eat or avoid, pikas tend to eat the plants livestock do not prefer [3, 33]. Li and colleagues found that pikas can slow the spread of unwanted plants and help the growth of grasses and sedges that livestock favor [33]. So on well-managed pastures, pikas do not compete with livestock for food. On badly damaged grazing land with a lot of pikas, there may be some competition, but pikas can still bring benefits for raising livestock.

One limitation of our study is that we did not go into the field to check directly what pikas eat. Reviewing earlier studies gives indirect evidence that their diet is flexible, but without our own data we cannot fully understand how pikas, plants and livestock affect one another. We therefore recommend that future studies use DNA metabarcoding. This method reads the DNA of plant remains in an animal's food or droppings to find out exactly which plants it ate. Using it across different regions and seasons would give a stronger scientific basis for managing several species together in high-mountain grasslands.

### How the grassland changed over the years under each approach

Our results show that neither pika control nor fencing led to large changes in the overall features of the grasslands (Figure 4). Still, after pika control was carried out in 2011 and 2012 (Table S7), the amount of plants livestock avoid went up significantly. This may be because pikas can hold back the growth of these avoided plants [30]. Once the pika population was reduced, those plants were free to grow more.

On the grazed land, which served as our comparison areas, several things first rose and then fell over time (Figure 4, Table S7). These were the number of species of plants livestock like to eat, the number of species of plants livestock don't like to eat, the total number of plant species, and the amount of plants livestock avoid. We think this pattern mainly comes from the same two effects of grazing described above: plants filling in around one another, and certain plants doing especially well. When enough light reached the ground, the niches left empty by grazing were slowly filled by plants that help the grassland recover, and the number of plant species went up [34, 35, 36]. Because livestock are choosy about what they eat, the plants they avoid gradually took over these empty niches, so the amount of those plants increased. Over time, the grassland's natural ability to bounce back caused the number of plant species and the grassland's stability to fall, until they finally leveled off.

### Limitations of the study

Our monitoring network covered a long time span (14 years) and a wide area (22 natural regions). Even so, there are several limitations to keep in mind when reading our findings.

First, although our study covers many kinds of high-mountain meadow, most of our sites were in the southeast of Qinghai Province. This is mainly because the northwest is mostly empty Gobi desert and bare land, without the grassland plants needed for grazing or for monitoring plants. So the long-term changes we found may not apply directly to these drier, thinly vegetated northwestern areas, or to other high-altitude places that are quite different.

Second, an important gap in explaining how things work is that we had no diet data for plateau pikas collected directly in the field at our own sites. Earlier studies and other ecological signs give a basis for our conclusions. But without detailed diet information, such as from DNA metabarcoding, we cannot understand in fine detail how pikas and livestock affect each other.

Finally, we did not measure how local money matters, living conditions and how willingly communities followed the rules affected the way these policies were carried out. These factors could add further complexity to the ecological results we saw.

parts.title: Killing plateau pikas harms grasslands, and fencing out livestock does not make them better
parts.abstract:
Summary

Two main tools are used to fight grassland damage on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau: controlling plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae, small burrowing mammals) and building fences to keep livestock out. To see how well they work, we studied 14 years of monitoring data from 1,460 plots across 22 ecoregions. We used a method called structural equation modeling, which maps how one change leads to another. It showed that reducing pika numbers had a weak, indirect, negative effect on how stable the grassland was. Neither long-term pika control nor fencing produced significant overall improvements. In other words, any differences we saw were too large to be explained easily by chance, but overall there were none like that.

Some grazing regimes did give an early boost. Plant richness (the number of plant species) rose by 18.7% for both palatable grasses (those livestock like to eat) and non-palatable grasses (those they do not prefer). The biomass of non-palatable grasses (the dry weight of plants) rose by 27.4%. But these gains faded after 8–10 years and returned to where they started. We conclude that pika control applied everywhere, without care, lowers habitat quality and brings no lasting benefit. We also conclude that large-scale fencing does not significantly improve grassland richness or stability. Relying on one single intervention is therefore not the best approach. We recommend management that combines several methods and adapts to local ecology.

Subject areas: environmental science, environmental management, agricultural science

parts.introduction_rest:
For a long time, people who manage grasslands have treated plateau pikas as pests that compete with livestock for grass.3,11,12,13 This view has led to large control programs. In Mongolia, controlling Brandt's vole has cost between $300,000 and $800,000 every year.1,14 In China, large-scale rodent control began in the 1960s. Over the decades the poisons have changed, from zinc phosphide to NH4+–fluoroacetate, and now to anticoagulants (poisons that stop blood from clotting, such as diphacinone-Na) and botulin toxin C.15 China's Ministry of Agriculture reported that 38,000 tons of rodent poison were used each year from 2003 to 2005.3,16

Recent ecological research, however, shows a more mixed picture. Pikas act as ecosystem engineers: their burrowing lets air into the soil and helps nutrients move through it.17 Under some conditions, the way they pick what to eat may hold back plants that animals do not like and help grass-like plants grow.18 This complexity is why we think it is time to take a fresh look at how pikas are managed.

Fencing is another common way to repair damaged pastures. It is popular because it is cheap and can be built over huge areas.8,19 China's program of returning grazing land to grassland, which began in 2003 and continues today, has fenced 57,600 km2 of damaged alpine grassland in northern Tibet to keep livestock out.20 In 2011 the program grew when a subsidy began paying herders 90 RMB per hectare per year (12 USD per hectare per year) to fence damaged pastures.5 Even so, nobody has yet checked carefully what ecological good this fencing does.3,5,8

So there is still a lot we do not know about these efforts. We do not know whether they work across large areas, or whether their benefits last over time. Small studies are plentiful, but broad studies that cover many regions and long periods are rare.9,10 To answer these questions, we set up a long-term monitoring network across 22 ecoregions, which together make up 85% of China's alpine meadow biome (the cold, high-elevation grassland zone). We followed it for 14 years, from 2005 to 2018. We monitored 1,460 plots, chosen at random within each region and located precisely, with an average of 66.3 plots per region.

We asked three main questions. First, how does fencing over large areas change the way plant communities develop over time, and the benefits that grasslands give people? Second, when plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae) are controlled for a long time, does this lead to a lasting change in the food chain, or does it only move the problem somewhere else? Third, in grasslands that do not settle into a steady state, how long does it take before a management method stops working as well?

## Methods (STAR format)

This table lists the data and software we used, where each came from, and where to find it.

| ggplot2 R package | Wickham40 | https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org |
| BioRender | BioRender.com | https://biorender.com/ |

### The animal we studied

The animal at the center of our study is the plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae), a small mammal found only on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We did not look at whether the results differed between male and female pikas. The pika control was carried out on whole populations within particular ecoregions, and we measured the effects on the plant community as a whole, not on individual animals. All field observations involving animals followed institutional permissions and oversight for animal welfare.

### Method details

#### Study site

Our study took place in Qinghai Province, on the northeast Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Figure 1). This is a high-altitude region, usually between 3000 and 5000 meters above sea level.41,42 The continental climate is harsh. The mean annual temperature is below freezing (historically 0°C, and -0.5°C during the study period, 2005-2018). Average yearly rainfall is 540 mm, and 70% of it falls from June to August (Figure 1).

The soils are mainly alpine meadow, scrub meadow, and bog types.43 They support alpine meadows, shrublands, and steppes, where the dominant plants are Carex spp., Kobresia spp., Stipa spp., Achantherum splendens, and Potentilla fruticose.44

#### Experimental design

We chose three common ways of managing grassland. The first is winter and summer grazing pastures, which served as our comparison group (Control). The second is long-term total fencing (Fence). The third is plateau pika control (Figure 1).

In May 2005, we set up 62 experimental areas across several counties in Qinghai. Each area was larger than 20 hectares (500 m × 400 m). We kept each management measure going through multi-year cycles of more than 3 years (Table S1). The sites had the rolling ground and sparse vegetation typical of grazed alpine pastures.

We set grazing levels using the Chinese agricultural industry code NY/T 635-2015 on carrying capacity (how many animals a pasture can support). On the advice of local grassland stations, we kept grassland use the same at all sites, at about 1.0 yak per hectare (a feeding rate of 45%–55%). To keep livestock out, we put up permanent wire mesh fences more than 15 cm above the ground. This height keeps out large grazing animals but lets small animals, such as microtine rodents (voles and similar rodents), pass underneath.

We chose thirty sites for pika management because no pika control had been done there before (Table S1). We applied pika control to a surrounding buffer zone of more than 20 hectares. Inside each zone, we marked out a central sampling area of less than 5 hectares for our measurements. To reduce pika numbers, we placed wheat bait treated with botulin C directly into pika burrows.

#### Field survey

In each study area, we randomly placed five plots of 10 m × 10 m, at least 50 m apart. These plots were set up temporarily. Every plot sat more than 20 m inside the edge of the habitat, so that conditions at the edge would not affect our results (the edge effect).

Inside each plot, we randomly placed three parallel 1 m × 1 m squares, called quadrats, for sampling plants (Table S2). The value for each 10 m × 10 m plot is the average of its three quadrats.

We sorted plant species into three groups: palatable grasses, non-palatable grasses, and avoidance grasses. The sorting followed the eating preferences of local livestock, especially yaks. We worked this out from regional plant guides and from interviews with local herders about what yaks choose to eat.45,46

To measure plant biomass, we cut all the plants at ground level inside each quadrat. We then dried them in an oven at 65 °C for 48 hours, until their weight stopped changing. We weighed the dry plant material on a precision balance that reads to 0.1 g. We monitored the sites every year in late July, when vegetation is at its seasonal peak. This let us compare the standing plant biomass fairly from one survey year to the next.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Grassland index calculation

We defined plant richness as the total number of species found in each 1 m × 1 m quadrat. We measured ecosystem stability with the Inverse Coefficient of Variation (ICV),47 which is the average biomass divided by how much it varies over time. A higher value means biomass stayed steadier from year to year. The formula is:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here μ is the mean aboveground biomass over the experimental years, and σ is the standard deviation of aboveground biomass over time. The standard deviation tells us how far the yearly values typically drift from their average.

#### Statistical analysis

We ran all analyses in R (version 4.3.0). We used linear mixed-effects models, fitted with the 'lmer' function in the 'lme4' package (version 1.1.33). These models let us ask how climate and management affect plant richness, stability, and biomass for each of the three grass groups (avoidance, non-palatable, and palatable).

In the models, the factors we wanted to test were the management measure (control, fencing, or pika control), the climate variables (mean annual temperature and annual precipitation), and the ways these might combine (their interactions). These are called fixed effects. County was treated as a random effect, which allows for the fact that sites in the same county may resemble each other. For every model, the total sample size was n = 1,460 observations. This is the sum of the yearly measurements from all study plots over the experimental period.

For all the mixed-effects results, three asterisks (∗∗∗) mark results that are statistically significant, which we defined as p < 0.05. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would show up by chance less than 5% of the time. In our figures, summary plots show the mean ± SEM, meaning the average plus or minus its standard error (a measure of how precisely the average is known). Plots of change over time also include 95% confidence intervals, which show the range of uncertainty around each estimate.

We used structural equation modeling (SEM) to look at what lies behind changes in grassland stability. This method maps how one change leads to another. We ran it with the 'psem' function from the 'piecewiseSEM' package (version 2.3.0). We prepared the data with the 'dplyr' package (version 1.1.2).48 Most of the illustrations were made with BioRender.com.

## Results

## What the restoration measures did to grasslands

Controlling plateau pikas clearly raised plant richness (the number of plant species). The rise was statistically significant for all plants together, for palatable grasses, and for avoided grasses, which are plants that livestock steer clear of. "Statistically significant" here means that if pika control really made no difference, a gap this large would show up by chance less than 5% of the time. Compared with the grazed control areas, the effect estimates ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 (Figures 1 and 2).

Fencing out livestock did not show the same benefit. Fenced and control areas did not differ in richness for any of the four plant groups: all plants, avoided, non-palatable, and palatable. Fencing also caused no change in grassland stability or in biomass (the dry weight of plants) for any of the four groups, compared with the control. Pika control, on the other hand, had a positive effect on the biomass of avoided grasses (estimate = 1.85; Figure 2).

### Figure 1

**Where our study sites are and what they are like, in Qinghai Province**

(A) Boxplots show the mean annual temperature (MAT) and mean annual precipitation (MAP) across the study sites from 2005 to 2018. Each box covers the middle half of the values and marks the median. The whiskers reach out to 1.5 times the width of the box.

(B) Maps show where the study plots lie across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

(C) Field photographs show the three kinds of management: grazing (the control), plateau pika control (PC), and fencing (fence).

### Figure 2

**Effects of the restoration measures on richness, stability, and biomass**

Data are shown as mean ± SEM (n = 1,460 observations). SEM is the standard error of the mean, a measure of how far the average might shift if we sampled again. PC: plateau pika control; fence: livestock kept out by fencing. Asterisks (∗∗∗) mark statistical significance at p < 0.05, tested with linear mixed-effects models. Images were created using BioRender.com.

We also looked closely at two representative plots to see how plant communities responded. The first was a fenced plot, Banma96. Grass-like plants such as Poa annua and Elymas nutons dominated it (Table S1). Both the number of species and the biomass stayed stable from year to year in all palatability classes (Figure S2).

The second was a plot under pika control, Gande85. There, avoided grasses made up 6.25%–23.53% of all the plants, and Oxytropis ochrocephala Bunge was the main avoided species. Both the richness and the biomass of avoided grasses showed a significant upward trend (Figure S2). The total species abundance in the pika-controlled plot rose by 31.25%, compared with 6.25% in the fenced plot (Table S3).

Across the whole region, long-term fencing left grasslands in about the same condition as the control (Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). A closer look, though, showed that sites responded in different ways. Of 32 sites, 14 had significantly more total biomass with fencing (p < 0.05), while 18 had significantly less (p < 0.05). Grass richness rose significantly at 13 sites and fell significantly at 19 (both p < 0.05). Stability was not significantly affected at any site compared with the controls (p > 0.05; Table S6).

So long-term fencing had very little effect on grasslands at the large scale, but its effects varied from place to place at smaller scales.

## How pika control affects grassland stability indirectly

We used structural equation modeling to follow the chain of links from pika control to stability (Figure 3). Higher grassland stability was strongly associated with a drop in the biomass of avoided grasses (−0.23) and with an increase in the richness of non-palatable grasses (−0.20). The numbers are standardized coefficients, which put every link on the same scale so they can be compared.

Pika control had an indirect negative effect on stability. It worked mainly through changes in resources that altered the richness of avoided grasses. That in turn changed the biomass of avoided grasses, and in the end stability went down. The models fitted the data with statistical significance (p = 0.29) and explained 13% of the variation in grassland stability.

### Figure 3

**Structural equation model of how pika control works, based on our experimental data**

All arrows show significant pathways. The numbers on the arrows are standardized regression coefficients ("r" values). The signs show a positive relationship, a negative one, or one that goes both ways (±) (p = 0.29). Path diagrams were created using BioRender.com.

## How grasslands changed over time under each measure

Fencing had little effect on richness or stability between 2005 and 2018 (p > 0.05, not significant). Under pika control, by contrast, the biomass of palatable grasses rose significantly (p < 0.05). Pika control also raised the biomass of avoided grasses in 2011 and 2012 (p < 0.05). Overall, grasslands under both fencing and pika control went up and down over time (Figure 4; Table S7).

### Figure 4

**Changes over time in richness and biomass of the plant groups (all, avoided, non-palatable, and palatable) under three measures, 2005 to 2018**

The three measures are control (grazing), fence, and PC (pika control). Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals, the range in which the true value likely falls.

In the control (grazing) areas, several things grew significantly over the 14 years from 2005 to 2018. These were the richness of all plants, of palatable grasses, and of non-palatable grasses, and the biomass of avoided grasses. A significant decrease followed each rise. Taken together, the trend was still upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
Discussion

Grazing vs. fencing response

Our results show that long-term fencing kept grasslands in about the same condition as grazing that was left uncontrolled when we looked at the whole region. At the level of single sites, though, the responses differed. This matters because many studies test fencing on small plots and then assume the same result holds everywhere. Our data suggest that assumption is not safe. Responses varied a lot from site to site: nearly half of the sites had more biomass inside fences, while others had less (Table S6). Uniform management strategies therefore have clear limits in a landscape as varied as this one. Fencing does not seem to be simply good or simply bad. Its effect appears to depend on local conditions such as which plants grow there, the soil, and how the land was grazed in the past.

Generalizing from small fencing experiments may lead to inaccurate predictions,21,22 because small studies often lack the environmental context needed to judge a management measure realistically.23 We recommend that future assessments sample at several scales, so that they take into account how much the landscape varies from place to place. This would give more reliable guidance for conservation plans aimed at particular places, and it would respect the ecological variety found in grasslands.

We also need to point out where our monitoring network was located. Most of it lay in southeastern Qinghai Province. The northwest is mostly uninhabited Gobi desert, which has no grassland vegetation and is not suitable for grazing, so we could not collect data there. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau has very different local climates, so whether our conclusions apply to other regions needs further study. Research covering a wider area would help show whether these patterns hold across different climate and ecological zones.

Grazing vs. plateau pika control response

Plateau pika control is studied less often than fencing or grazing, yet it is widely used in many places to protect the grasses that livestock like to eat. Unlike grazing, pika control had no effect on the biomass of palatable grasses. It did, however, clearly increase both the richness and the biomass of avoidance grasses (those livestock leave alone), and this was statistically significant (p < 0.05). We think this comes from complementary and selective effects. Under long-term grazing, palatable grasses were held back, and where pikas were controlled, avoidance grasses moved into the spaces (ecological niches) those grasses left empty24,25 (Figure S1). But more avoidance-grass biomass lowered the overall stability of the grassland (Figure 3). So using pika control on its own may be unwise. It could damage wildlife habitat and give little benefit to livestock.

These findings challenge the common belief that plateau pikas increase avoidance grasses and reduce palatable ones26,27,28,29 (see Figures 2 and 3; Figure S1; Table S4). We began this study from the view that pikas on the plateau compete with livestock for food and damage rangelands. The evidence, however, points to a more nuanced relationship. Plateau pikas are choosy feeders, and what they eat does not necessarily clash with what livestock eat.30 They mainly eat grasses and sedges, but they also eat many broad-leaved herbs, including legumes. For example, an analysis of stomach contents under the microscope showed that Oxytropis plants (including O. glabra and O. kansuensis) made up a large part of the diet of plateau pikas in meadows dominated by Elymus nutans.31 These legumes contain alkaloids and other chemicals that normally discourage animals from eating them. Plateau pikas seem to get around this with specialized microbes in their gut, which lets them cope with the chemistry of plants in high-altitude grasslands.32

Their diet also changes with the seasons, and they eat a wider range of plants in the cold months. Potentilla anserina is an important food then, which shows how pikas adjust their feeding as conditions change. In fact, when overgrazing causes poorly palatable or avoidance grasses to spread, plateau pikas tend to eat plants that livestock do not prefer.3,33 Li et al. found that plateau pikas can slow the spread of unwanted plants and help the grasses and sedges that livestock favor to grow.33 So in well-managed pastures, plateau pikas do not compete with livestock for food. In heavily degraded rangelands with many pikas, some competition may occur, but pikas can still benefit livestock production.

One limitation is that we did not study the diet of plateau pikas directly in the field. Putting together the existing literature gives indirect evidence that their diet is flexible, but without our own data we cannot fully understand how these species affect each other. We therefore recommend that future work use DNA metabarcoding, a method that identifies the plants an animal has eaten from traces of DNA, to build precise diet profiles across regions and seasons. This would give a firmer scientific basis for managing several species together in alpine grasslands.

Changes over time under different measures

Pika control and fencing did not lead to substantial changes in the overall character of the grasslands (Figure 4). There was one exception. After pika control began in 2011 and 2012 (Table S7), the biomass of avoidance grasses increased significantly. This may be because plateau pikas hold back the growth of avoidance grasses,30 so once pika numbers fell, these plants grew more.

Under grazing (the Control), richness of palatable grasses, of non-palatable grasses and of all grasses together, as well as the biomass of avoidance grasses, first rose and then fell over time (Figure 4; Table S7). We think this is mainly due to complementary and selective effects of grazing. Where there was enough light, the niches emptied by grazing were gradually filled by recovering plants, and richness went up.34,35,36 Because livestock choose what they eat, avoidance grasses then slowly took over the empty niches, and their biomass increased. Over time, the grassland ecosystem's resilience caused richness and stability to decline and eventually level off.

Limitations of the study

Our monitoring network is strong in both time (14 years) and space (22 ecoregions). Even so, several limits should be kept in mind when reading our findings. First, our study covers a broad range of alpine meadow types, but it was centered mainly on southeastern Qinghai Province. This is largely because the northwest is mostly uninhabited Gobi desert and barren land, which has no grassland vegetation for grazing and monitoring. So the patterns of change we found may not carry over directly to these drier, sparsely vegetated northwestern areas or to other distinct high-altitude ecosystems.

Second, we have no primary, site-specific data on what plateau pikas eat from direct field work. Existing literature and ecological indicators support our conclusions, but without detailed diet profiling, such as DNA metabarcoding, we cannot understand in finer detail how pikas and livestock affect each other.

Finally, we did not measure how local social and economic conditions, or how well communities followed the policies, affected the way these measures were carried out. These factors could add further complexity to the ecological outcomes we observed.

parts.title: Reducing plateau pika numbers damages grasslands, while fencing out grazing animals does not improve their habitat
parts.abstract:
Summary

Reducing the numbers of plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae), small mammals native to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and putting up fences to keep grazing animals out are two main ways managers try to restore damaged grasslands there. We analyzed 14 years of monitoring data from 1,460 study plots across 22 ecological regions—areas with different environmental conditions. We used a statistical model that examines both direct links and links that work through other changes. It showed that reducing pika numbers had a weak, indirect negative effect on grassland stability: how steady the amount of plant material above ground stays over time. Neither long-term pika control nor fencing led to statistically significant improvements overall. In other words, we could not show an overall improvement that met the statistical test; this does not prove there was none.

Under certain grazing patterns, the number of plant species that livestock like to eat and those they do not like to eat initially rose by 18.7%. The amount of plant material from grasses livestock do not like to eat rose by 27.4%. But these gains faded after 8–10 years, returning to their starting levels. These findings demonstrate that reducing plateau pika numbers without considering local needs damages habitat quality without lasting benefits. They also show that large-scale fencing does not bring statistically significant improvements in the number of grassland plant species or in grassland stability. Our results suggest that relying on single actions is not the best approach. Instead, we need to combine management methods and adjust them to local conditions and changes in the environment.

Subject areas: environmental science, environmental management, agricultural science
parts.introduction_first: Managing the environment brings a basic tension: science needs to test ideas carefully, while people making policies need answers they can act on. [1,2] This tension is especially clear when managing natural systems. Changes in one part of a system can affect other parts and feed back on the original change in complicated ways, [3] while social and economic pressures demand quick solutions. [1] China’s grazing lands, which cover 4 million km², show this challenge clearly. Fencing programs, now in place for more than 25 years, and large-scale programs to reduce plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae) numbers have dominated grassland restoration efforts since 2000. [4,5] These programs have received more than 12 billion in funding since 2010 and cover 78% of damaged grasslands. Yet scientists still debate whether they make ecological sense and can work well over the long term. [6–10] Growing evidence suggests that they can have unexpected effects. These include disrupting chains of effects through the food web—where changes in one species affect the others linked to it through feeding—[3] and making landscapes more alike, with less variety from place to place. [4] Such effects challenge the basic assumptions behind current management approaches.

Managers have traditionally treated plateau pikas as pasture pests that compete with livestock for plants to eat. [3,11–13] This view has led to large control programs. [15] According to China’s Ministry of Agriculture, 38,000 tons of rodent poison were used each year from 2003 to 2005. [3,16] Yet recent ecological research shows that pikas play more complex roles. By digging burrows, they help air move through the soil and nutrients cycle through the environment. In this way, they act as “ecosystem engineers”—animals that reshape their surroundings. [17] Under certain conditions, their choices about which plants to eat may limit plants livestock do not like to eat and help grasses and grass-like plants grow. [18] These varied effects show why we need to rethink how we manage pikas.

Fencing remains a common way to restore damaged pastures because it is cost-effective and can be used over large areas. [8,19] China’s returning grazing land to grassland initiative, which began in 2003 and continues today, has fenced 57,600 km² of damaged high-altitude grasslands in northern Tibet to keep livestock out. [20] A subsidy program expanded this effort in 2011, paying herders 90 RMB per hectare each year (12 USD per hectare each year) to fence damaged pastures. [5] However, the benefits of this fencing for the natural environment have not been thoroughly assessed. [3,5,8]

We still face major questions about whether current grassland management methods work across large areas and whether their benefits last. Many studies cover small areas, but few assess several ecological regions over long periods. [9,10] To answer these questions, we set up a monitoring network across 22 ecological regions, representing 85% of China’s high-altitude meadow habitat. We monitored these areas over 14 yearly cycles, from 2005 to 2018. We tracked conditions and locations at 1,460 study plots, chosen randomly within defined groups to represent the study area, with an average of 66.3 plots per region. (2) Does continually reducing plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae) numbers lead to lasting changes in the food web—who eats what—or merely shift the signs of a problem elsewhere? (3) In grasslands that keep changing rather than settling into a steady state, at what points in time do management methods lose their effectiveness?

[45,46] For each 10 m × 10 m plot, we calculated plant-community measurements by averaging the values from its three sampling squares.

To measure the amount of plant material, we cut all vegetation at ground level within each sampling square. We then dried it in an oven at 65°C for 48 hours, until its mass no longer changed. We weighed the dried material on a precise balance that could measure in steps of 0.1 g. We repeated this monitoring each year in late July, when vegetation was at its seasonal peak. Using the same timing allowed us to compare the amount of plant material present across survey years.

## Measurements and statistical analysis

### Calculating grassland measures

We measured the number of plant species, also called species richness, by counting all the species identified within each 1 m × 1 m sampling square. To describe ecosystem stability—how steady the amount of plant material above ground stays over time—we used the Inverse Coefficient of Variation (ICV). [47] We calculated it as:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here, μ is the average amount of plant material above ground over the experimental years. The symbol σ is its standard deviation over time, a measure of how widely the yearly amounts vary around that average. Thus, this stability measure compares the average amount with how much it changes over time.

### Statistical analysis

We ran our statistical analyses in R (version 4.3.0). We used linear mixed-effects models, which let us examine the factors of interest while accounting for differences among counties. We built these models with the ‘lmer’ function in the ‘lme4’ package (version 1.1.33). We measured how climate and management affected the number of plant species, stability, and amount of plant material across the three feeding-preference groups: grasses livestock avoid, do not like to eat, and like to eat.

The models treated management approach—control, fencing, or reducing plateau pika numbers—and climate—mean yearly temperature and yearly precipitation—as fixed effects, meaning factors whose effects we wanted to estimate directly. We also included their interactions: whether the effect of one factor changed depending on another. We treated county as a random effect, allowing for background differences among counties. Every statistical model used a total sample size of n = 1,460 observations. These were the accumulated yearly measurements across all study plots over the experimental period.

For all linear mixed-effects model results, three asterisks (∗∗∗) indicate statistical significance at p < 0.05. This means that, if there were really no effect, a result at least this extreme would appear by chance less than 5% of the time. In all summary graphs, we show the mean ± SEM. SEM means standard error of the mean and describes the uncertainty in the estimated average. Graphs showing change over time include 95% confidence intervals, which show uncertainty around the estimates. Over repeated studies using the same method, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value.

We also used structural equation modeling (SEM), a statistical model that examines both direct links and links that work through other changes, to analyze the processes behind changes in grassland stability. We ran this analysis with the ‘psem’ function in the ‘piecewiseSEM’ package (version 2.3.0). We used the ‘dplyr’ package (version 1.1.2) to organize and process the data. [48] We created most graphical illustrations using BioRender.com.

## Results

### How restoration measures affected grasslands

Reducing plateau pika numbers increased the number of plant species overall, the number livestock like to eat, and the number livestock avoid eating. These increases were statistically significant (p < 0.05), with estimated effects ranging from 1.56 to 1.92 compared with the grazing control areas (Figures 1 and 2). A result is statistically significant at this level when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time. In contrast, fenced areas and control areas did not differ in the number of species in any of the four groups: all plants, plants livestock avoid, plants livestock do not like to eat, and plants they like to eat. Fencing also caused no changes in grassland stability—how steady the amount of plant material above ground stays over time—or in the amount of aboveground plant material in any of these four groups compared with the control. Reducing pika numbers also had a positive effect on the amount of aboveground plant material from plants livestock avoid eating, with an estimated effect of 1.85 (Figure 2).

Figure 1
