(A) Boxplots show mean annual temperature (MAT) and mean annual precipitation (MAP) across study sites from 2005 to 2018. Each box shows the middle half of the values, called the interquartile range (IQR), and marks the median, or middle value. The lines extending from the boxes reach to 1.5 × IQR.

(B) Maps show where the study plots lie across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

(C) Field photographs show examples of the three management approaches: grazing (control), reducing plateau pika numbers (PC), and fencing out grazing animals (fence).

Figure 2

Effects of restoration measures on the number of plant species, grassland stability, and the amount of aboveground plant material (AGB)

Values are means ± the standard error of the mean (SEM), which describes uncertainty in the estimated mean (n = 1,460 observations). PC means reducing plateau pika numbers; fence means fencing out grazing animals. Asterisks (∗∗∗) mark statistically significant results at p < 0.05 from linear mixed-effects models, statistical tools that compare management effects while accounting for grouped observations. Images were created using BioRender.com.

We examined plant community responses to management in two representative plots. In the fenced plot, Banma96, grass-like plants such as Poa annua and Elymas nutons dominated (Table S1). Both the number of species and the amount of plant material in every livestock feeding-preference group remained stable from year to year (Figure S2). In Gande85, where pika numbers were reduced, plants livestock avoid eating made up 6.25%–23.53% of the total plant community. Oxytropis ochrocephala Bunge was the dominant species in this group. This plot also showed a statistically significant upward trend in both the number of species and the amount of plant material in the group livestock avoid (Figure S2). The increase in total species abundance was larger in the plot where pika numbers were reduced, at 31.25%, than in the fenced plot, at 6.25% (Table S3).

Across the region, long-term fencing kept overall grassland conditions similar to those in the grazing control areas (Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). Yet a closer look showed that responses differed among sites. At 14 of the 32 sites, fencing increased the total amount of plant material compared with the control; at the other 18 sites, it decreased. Both sets of changes were statistically significant (p < 0.05). The number of grass species increased at 13 sites and decreased at 19, again with statistically significant changes (p < 0.05). At every site, stability showed no statistically significant change compared with the control (p > 0.05; Table S6). This means we could not show a difference in stability, not that we proved there was none. These findings show that long-term fencing had little effect on grasslands across the region as a whole, but its effects varied at smaller, local scales.

### Indirect effects of reducing plateau pika numbers on grassland stability

Greater grassland stability was strongly linked to a decline in the amount of plant material from plants livestock avoid eating (−0.23) and an increase in the number of species livestock do not like to eat (−0.20) (Figure 3). Reducing plateau pika numbers had an indirect negative effect on stability. This happened mainly through a chain of changes: management changed resources, which affected the number of plant species livestock avoid, then the amount of plant material in that group, and finally reduced grassland stability. We examined this chain using a statistical model that examines both direct links and links that work through other changes, called structural equation modeling. The models showed a statistically significant fit to the data for explaining grassland stability (p = 0.29). They explained 13% of the variation in stability.

Figure 3

A model of the direct and indirect effects of reducing plateau pika numbers, based on experimental data

All arrows show statistically significant links. The numbers on the arrows are standardized regression coefficients (“r” values): they describe the strength and direction of links on a shared scale. The signs show positive (+), negative (−), or bimodal (±) relationships, meaning relationships with two patterns (p = 0.29). Path diagrams were created using BioRender.com.

### Changes in grasslands over time under different measures

Between 2005 and 2018, fencing had little effect on the number of plant species or on grassland stability, with no statistically significant changes (p > 0.05). In contrast, reducing plateau pika numbers produced a statistically significant increase in the amount of plant material from grasses livestock like to eat (p < 0.05). Reducing pika numbers also increased the amount of plant material from grasses livestock avoid eating in 2011 and 2012; these increases were statistically significant (p < 0.05). Overall, grasslands under both fencing and reduced pika numbers fluctuated over time (Figure 4; Table S7).

Figure 4

Changes from 2005 to 2018 in plant diversity and the amount of plant material in four groups—all plants, plants livestock avoid, plants they do not like to eat, and plants they like to eat—under grazing (control), fencing (fence), and reduced plateau pika numbers (PC)

Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals, which indicate uncertainty around the estimates.

In the grazing control areas, total grassland, grasses livestock like to eat, the number of species livestock do not like to eat, and the amount of plant material from grasses livestock avoid all increased significantly over the 14-year period (2005–2018). These increases were followed by statistically significant decreases, but the overall trend was upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

### Grazing compared with fencing

Our findings show that, across the region, long-term fencing kept grasslands in conditions similar to those under uncontrolled grazing. Yet the response differed from place to place. This difference between local and regional results challenges the common practice of using small fencing studies to predict what will happen across larger areas. Nearly half of the sites had more plant material, while others had less. These mixed responses show the limits of applying the same management strategy across landscapes with different conditions (Table S6). Rather than always helping or always harming grasslands, fencing appears to work differently depending on local conditions, such as the mix of plants, soil properties, and past grazing.

Using small fencing experiments to make broad predictions may give misleading answers. [21,22] Small studies often lack the wider environmental context needed to judge realistically how management actions will work. [23] We therefore recommend that future assessments collect data at several scales, from individual sites to wider landscapes, and account for differences across the landscape. This would provide more reliable guidance for conservation strategies suited to the varied conditions found in grasslands.

Our monitoring network was mainly in southeastern Qinghai Province. The northwestern areas are mostly uninhabited Gobi desert, without grassland vegetation. These conditions are unsuitable for grazing, so we could not collect data there. Because local climates vary greatly across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, further research is needed to find out how widely our conclusions apply elsewhere. Research covering a larger geographical area would help test whether these patterns hold across areas with different ecological and climate conditions.

### Grazing compared with reducing plateau pika numbers

Reducing plateau pika numbers is less often studied than fencing or grazing, but managers widely use it to protect grasses livestock like to eat. Compared with grazing, reducing pika numbers had no effect on the amount of these grasses. Instead, it led to a marked, statistically significant increase in both the number of species and the amount of aboveground plant material among grasses livestock avoid (p < 0.05). A result is statistically significant at this level when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would occur by chance alone less than 5% of the time. We attribute this response to plants using different resources and to some plants gaining an advantage over others. In areas where pika numbers were reduced, prolonged grazing had held back grasses livestock like to eat. Grasses livestock avoid could then use the space and resources left available. [24,25] (Figure S1). However, the increase in plant material from grasses livestock avoid reduced grassland stability—how steady the amount of plant material above ground stays over time (Figure 3). Reducing pika numbers on its own may therefore be unwise: it could damage wildlife habitats while offering little benefit to livestock.

These findings challenge the usual view that plateau pikas increase grasses livestock avoid and decrease grasses livestock like to eat. [26–29] (See Figures 2 and 3; Figure S1; Table S4.) Our study began with the widespread assumption that plateau pikas compete with livestock for food and contribute to damage to grazing lands. However, the evidence suggests a more complex relationship. Plateau pikas choose particular plants to eat, and their diet does not necessarily overlap with the forage livestock need. [30] Although they mainly eat grasses and sedges, they also eat many broad-leaved herbs, including legumes, the plant family that includes peas and beans. For example, researchers examined tiny plant remains in pika stomachs under a microscope. They found that Oxytropis species, including O. glabra and O. kansuensis, made up a substantial part of the diet in meadows dominated by Elymus nutans. [31] These legumes contain alkaloids and other plant chemicals that usually discourage animals from eating them. Plateau pikas appear to counter these chemicals with the help of specialized microbes in their gut. This allows them to adapt their diet to the distinctive mix of plant chemicals in high-altitude grasslands. [32]

Pika diets also change with the seasons, with a wider variety of plants eaten during cold seasons. Potentilla anserina makes up a notable part of their diet at this time, showing how they adjust their feeding as conditions change. In fact, when overgrazing allows plants that livestock dislike or avoid to spread, plateau pikas tend to eat those plants. [3,33] Li and colleagues found that plateau pikas can slow the spread of unwanted plants and encourage the growth of grasses and grass-like plants, including sedges, that livestock favor. [33] Therefore, in well-managed pastures, plateau pikas do not compete with livestock for food. Some competition may occur in heavily damaged grazing lands with many pikas, but pikas can still benefit livestock production.

One limitation of our study is that we did not directly investigate pika diets in the field. Combining evidence from published studies gives indirect support for their ability to change their diet, but the lack of our own dietary data limits our understanding of how pikas and livestock affect one another. We recommend that future research use DNA metabarcoding—a method that identifies foods from traces of their DNA—to measure pika diets precisely across regions and seasons. This would give a stronger scientific basis for managing several species together in alpine grasslands.

### How grasslands change over time under different management methods

Our findings indicate that reducing plateau pika numbers and fencing did not substantially change the overall characteristics of the grasslands (Figure 4). However, after actions to reduce pika numbers in 2011 and 2012 (Table S7), the amount of plant material from grasses livestock avoid increased significantly. This may be because plateau pikas can hold back the growth of these grasses. [30] Once pika numbers fell, the amount of these plants therefore increased.

Under grazing conditions (Control), the number of species that livestock like to eat, the number they do not like to eat, and the total number of grassland plant species first rose and then fell over time. The amount of plant material from grasses livestock avoid followed the same pattern (Figure 4; Table S7). We mainly attribute this pattern to the different ways plants use resources and to livestock choosing some plants over others. Where enough light was available, recovering plants gradually filled the spaces and used the resources left available by grazing, increasing the number of plant species. [34–36] Because livestock choose which plants to eat, grasses they avoid gradually took over these openings, increasing the amount of plant material from those grasses. Over time, the grassland ecosystem's resilience—its ability to respond to disturbance—caused the number of species and grassland stability to fall and eventually level off.

### Limitations of the study

Our monitoring network covered a long period, 14 years, and a wide area, 22 ecological regions. Even so, several limitations matter when interpreting these findings. First, although we studied a broad range of alpine meadow environments, our sites were mainly in southeastern Qinghai Province. This was largely because the northwestern areas are mostly uninhabited Gobi desert and barren land. They lack the grassland vegetation needed for grazing and ecological monitoring. The patterns of change in grassland communities that we identified may therefore not apply directly to those drier northwestern areas with little vegetation, or to other distinct high-altitude ecosystems.

Second, we did not collect direct field data on plateau pika diets at our study sites, which limits our understanding of the processes behind our results. Published research and signs of ecological change provide a basis for our conclusions. However, without detailed diet measurements, such as those provided by DNA metabarcoding, we cannot understand the interactions between pikas and livestock in as much detail. Finally, we did not directly measure how differences in local social and economic conditions, or in how closely communities followed the policies, affected their implementation. These factors could add further complexity to the ecological outcomes we observed.

parts.title: Controlling plateau pikas harms grasslands, while fencing out grazing animals does not improve their habitat
parts.abstract:
Summary

Controlling plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae) and putting up fences to keep grazing animals out are two main ways people try to restore damaged grasslands on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We examined 14 years of records from 1,460 plots across 22 ecological regions to see how well these approaches worked. A model that traced links among changes in the grassland showed that reducing pika numbers had a weak, indirect negative effect on grassland stability—how steady plant growth remained over time. Neither long-term pika control nor fencing brought statistically significant overall improvements. Under some grazing approaches, the number of kinds of grasses that livestock eat and avoid initially rose by 18.7%, and the amount of grass that livestock do not favor rose by 27.4%. After 8–10 years, those gains faded back to their starting levels. Our findings show that controlling pikas without regard to local conditions harms habitat quality without lasting benefits, while large-scale fencing does not significantly improve the number of plant kinds or grassland stability. We suggest moving away from reliance on either measure alone and toward approaches that combine methods and adapt to local conditions.

Subject areas: environmental science, environmental management, agricultural science
parts.introduction_first: The way science works can clash with the need to make policy decisions: researchers need time and evidence, while decision-makers often need to act quickly.1,2 Managing natural areas makes this especially difficult. Changes in plants and animals can set off further changes,3 while people also need solutions now.1 China’s grazing lands cover 4 million km² and show this challenge clearly. Since 2000, efforts to restore grasslands have been dominated by fencing, used for more than 25 years, and large-scale control of plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae).4,5 These measures have received more than 12 billion in funding since 2010 and have been used across 78% of damaged grasslands. Yet scientists still debate whether they make ecological sense and can work over the long term.6,7,8,9,10 Growing evidence points to unexpected results, including disruptions that spread through food webs3 and landscapes becoming more alike,4 calling the assumptions behind current management into question.
parts.introduction_rest:
Traditional grassland management has often treated plateau pikas as pasture pests that compete with livestock for food.3,11,12,13 This view has led to widespread efforts to reduce their numbers. In Mongolia, controlling Brandt’s vole, another grassland rodent, has cost $300,000–$800,000 each year.1,14 In China, large-scale rodent control began in the 1960s. The poisons used have ranged from zinc phosphide and NH4+–fluoroacetate to anticoagulants, such as diphacinone-Na, and botulin toxin C, which are now commonly used.15 China’s Ministry of Agriculture reported that 38,000 tons of rodenticide were used annually in each year from 2003 to 2005.3,16

More recent research shows that pikas do more than compete for food. Their digging makes space for air in the soil and helps nutrients move through it.17 By choosing which plants to eat, they may also hold back plants that livestock do not favor and help grasses and grass-like plants grow under certain conditions.18 These roles give us reason to reconsider how we manage pikas.

Fencing out grazing animals remains a common way to restore damaged pastures because it is relatively inexpensive and can be used across large areas.8,19 Since 2003, China’s initiative to return grazing land to grassland has fenced 57,600 km² of damaged high-altitude grassland in northern Tibet to keep livestock out.20 A subsidy scheme introduced in 2011 expanded the practice by paying herders 90 RMB per hectare per year (12 USD per hectare per year) to fence damaged pastures.5 Yet the ecological benefits of fencing have not been thoroughly assessed.3,5,8

We still do not know enough about whether these grassland measures work across large areas or whether their effects last. Many studies have examined small areas, but broad assessments across multiple ecological regions and many years remain scarce.9,10 To address these gaps, we monitored grasslands each year from 2005 through 2018—a 14-year period—across 22 ecological regions covering 85% of China’s high-altitude meadow areas. We followed 1,460 plots chosen at random within groups set up to represent different conditions, with an average of 66.3 plots per region. We asked three questions: (1) how fencing across a landscape changes the plants that grow there over time and the benefits grasslands provide; (2) whether sustained control of plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae) brings lasting changes to food-web relationships or simply shifts the problems elsewhere; and (3) how long these management measures remain effective in grasslands that do not stay in one fixed state.

Study animals and other study details

We studied plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae), small mammals native to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We did not analyze whether the animals’ sex affected the results: we managed pika populations across particular ecological regions and measured responses across whole plant communities. We carried out all animal-related field observations with institutional permission and oversight for animal welfare.

How we carried out the study

Study site

Our study took place in Qinghai Province on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Figure 1). The land is high, typically 3,000–5,000 meters above sea level.41,42 It has a harsh continental climate. The historical average yearly temperature was 0°C; during the 2005–2018 study period, it was −0.5°C. Average yearly precipitation was 540 mm, with 70% falling from June through August (Figure 1). The main soil types are alpine meadow, scrub meadow, and bog.43 They support alpine meadows, shrublands, and steppes dominated by Carex, Kobresia, and Stipa species, Achantherum splendens, and Potentilla fruticose.44

Experimental design

We compared three common ways of managing these grasslands: pastures grazed in winter and summer, which served as the control group; long-term fencing that kept grazing animals out; and controlling plateau pikas (Figure 1). In May 2005, we set up 62 study areas across several Qinghai counties. Each covered more than 20 hectares and measured 500 m × 400 m. We maintained the management measures through repeated cycles lasting more than three years (Table S1). The areas had the rolling land and sparse plants typical of grazed alpine pastures.

We set grazing levels according to the Chinese agricultural industry standard for how many animals the grassland can support, NY/T 635-2015. Following advice from local grassland stations, we kept grassland use at about 1.0 yak per hectare, with a feeding rate of 45%–55%, across all sites. Where we excluded grazing animals, we installed permanent wire-mesh fences more than 15 cm above the ground. These kept out large plant-eating animals but let small animals, such as microtine rodents, pass underneath.

We selected 30 pika management sites where no earlier pika control had taken place (Table S1). At each site, we treated a surrounding buffer zone larger than 20 hectares and set aside a central area smaller than 5 hectares for measurements. To reduce pika numbers, we placed wheat bait containing botulin C directly into pika burrows.

Field survey

In each study area, we temporarily marked five randomly placed plots, each 10 m × 10 m and at least 50 m from the next. We placed every plot more than 20 m inside the habitat boundary so that conditions at the edge would not affect the measurements. Within each plot, we randomly placed three parallel 1 m × 1 m squares to sample plants (Table S2). We grouped plant species by whether local livestock, especially yaks, preferred to eat them: grasses they eat, grasses they do not favor, and grasses they avoid. We based these groups on regional plant guides and interviews with local herders about how yaks feed.45,46 For each 10 m × 10 m plot, we averaged the measurements from its three smaller squares.

In every sampling square, we cut all plants at ground level. We then dried them in an oven at 65°C for 48 hours until their mass stopped changing and weighed the dry plant material on a balance that measured to 0.1 g. We repeated field measurements every year in late July, when plant growth was at its seasonal peak, so we could compare the amount of standing plant material across survey years on the same basis.

Measurements and statistical analysis

Calculating grassland measures

We counted the number of kinds of plants as the total number of species found in each 1 m × 1 m sampling square. To describe grassland stability—how steady above-ground plant biomass remained over the experimental years—we used the inverse coefficient of variation (ICV).47 We calculated it as:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here, μ is the mean above-ground biomass over the experimental years, and σ is the standard deviation of above-ground biomass over time—a measure of how much it varied.

Statistical analysis

We analyzed the data in R (version 4.3.0). Using the ‘lmer’ function in the ‘lme4’ package (version 1.1.33), we fitted linear mixed-effects models. These models let us examine management and climate together while allowing results to vary by county. We measured their effects on the number of kinds of plants, grassland stability, and plant biomass in three groups: grasses livestock avoid, grasses they do not favor, and grasses they eat. The management measures (control grazing, fencing, and pika control), climate measures (mean annual temperature and annual precipitation), and their interactions—whether the effect of one depended on another—were fixed effects. County was a random effect, allowing for differences among counties. Every statistical model used n = 1,460 observations: the annual measurements added together across all study plots during the experimental period. For all linear mixed-effects model results, three asterisks (∗∗∗) mark p < 0.05. We call a result statistically significant at that level when a difference this large would arise less than 5% of the time by chance alone if there were really no difference. In summary graphs, we show averages with ± SEM (standard error of the mean, a measure of how precisely we estimated an average). Graphs showing change over time include 95% confidence intervals, which show the uncertainty around the estimates.

We also used a model that traced links among changes in the grassland—structural equation modeling (SEM)—to examine what lay behind changes in grassland stability. We ran it with the ‘psem’ function in the ‘piecewiseSEM’ package (version 2.3.0). We used the ‘dplyr’ package (version 1.1.2) to work with the data.48 We created most illustrations with BioRender.com.

## Results

### How the restoration measures affected grasslands

Compared with the grazing control areas, areas where plateau pikas were controlled had a statistically significant higher number of kinds of plants overall, among plants livestock eat, and among plants livestock avoid (p < 0.05). The estimated effects ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 times the control values (Figures 1 and 2). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone—less than 5% of the time at p < 0.05. Fencing out grazing animals, by contrast, showed no difference from the control in the number of kinds of plants in any of the four groups: all plants, plants livestock avoid, plants livestock do not favor, and plants livestock eat. Fencing also showed no change from the control in grassland stability or aboveground plant mass for any of those groups. Pika control had a positive estimated effect of 1.85 on the aboveground mass of plants livestock avoid (Figure 2).

We looked more closely at how plant communities responded in two representative plots. In the fenced plot, Banma96, grass-like plants such as Poa annua and Elymas nutons dominated (Table S1). From year to year, the number of kinds of plants and their mass stayed steady across all groups classified by whether livestock eat them (Figure S2). In the pika-control plot, Gande85, plants livestock avoid made up 6.25%–23.53% of the total plant community. Oxytropis ochrocephala Bunge was the dominant species in that group. The number of kinds and the mass of plants livestock avoid both showed a statistically significant upward trend there (Figure S2). Total plant abundance increased by 31.25% in the pika-control plot, compared with 6.25% in the fenced plot (Table S3).

Across the region, grassland conditions after prolonged fencing remained comparable to those in the grazing control areas (Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). Individual sites, however, responded differently. With fencing, total plant mass increased at 14 of 32 sites and decreased at 18; both sets of changes were statistically significant (p < 0.05). The number of kinds of grasses increased at 13 sites and decreased at 19, again with statistically significant changes (p < 0.05). Compared with controls, grassland stability showed no statistically significant change at any site (p > 0.05; Table S6). Thus, long-term fencing had little effect at the regional scale, but its effects differed among sites.

### How plateau pika control indirectly affected grassland stability

Greater grassland stability was strongly associated with less mass of plants livestock avoid (−0.23) and more kinds of plants livestock do not favor (−0.20) (Figure 3). Our model tracing links among changes in the grassland showed that controlling plateau pikas had an indirect negative effect on stability: the intervention affected the number of kinds of plants livestock avoid, which in turn affected their mass and ultimately reduced stability. The model fit the data according to the reported test (p = 0.29) and explained 13% of the variation in grassland stability.

### How grasslands changed over time under different measures

From 2005 to 2018, fencing had little effect on the number of kinds of plants or on grassland stability; these differences were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). By contrast, controlling plateau pikas significantly increased the mass of plants livestock eat (p < 0.05). It also significantly increased the mass of plants livestock avoid in 2011 and 2012 (p < 0.05). Overall, the grasslands under both fencing and pika control fluctuated over time (Figure 4; Table S7).

Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals, which indicate uncertainty around the trends.

In the grazing control areas, total grassland, plants livestock eat, and the number of kinds of plants livestock do not favor, along with the mass of plants livestock avoid, rose significantly during the 14 years from 2005 to 2018. They then fell significantly, but the overall trend was upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

### Grazing compared with fencing out grazing animals

Across the region, grasslands fenced for a long time remained much like those with unrestricted grazing. At individual sites, though, the responses differed. Nearly half the sites gained plant biomass—the amount of plant material—while others lost it (Table S6). This difference between local and regional results challenges the practice of using small fencing studies to predict what will happen across a wider area. Fencing did not produce the same positive or negative result everywhere. Its effects appear to depend on local conditions, including which plants grow there, soil properties, and the area's grazing history.

Drawing broad conclusions from a few small fencing experiments may therefore lead to inaccurate predictions.21,22 Such experiments often miss the wider environmental setting needed to judge how a management measure will work.23 We recommend that future assessments measure grasslands at both local and landscape scales and account for differences across the landscape. That would give more reliable guidance for conservation plans suited to different grasslands.

Most sites in our monitoring network were in southeastern Qinghai Province. Northwestern Qinghai is mostly uninhabited Gobi desert, without the grassland vegetation needed for grazing, so we could not collect data there. Because local climates vary greatly across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, more research is needed before applying our conclusions to other regions. Studies covering a wider area could test whether these patterns also hold in different climates and ecological settings.

### Grazing compared with controlling plateau pikas

Although researchers have studied pika control less often than fencing or grazing, people use it widely in various places to protect grasses that livestock favor. Unlike grazing, controlling pikas did not affect the amount of these favored grasses. Instead, it brought a marked, statistically significant increase in both the number of kinds and the aboveground amount of grasses that livestock avoid (p < 0.05). A result is called statistically significant at this level when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time. This increase can be explained by different plants using available space and resources in different ways: after prolonged grazing had held back favored grasses in pika-control areas, grasses livestock avoid filled the openings they left.24,25 (Figure S1). But the increase in grasses livestock avoid reduced grassland stability—how steady plant growth remained over time (Figure 3). We therefore advise against using pika control alone: it could damage wildlife habitat while offering limited benefits to livestock.

These results challenge the common view that pikas cause grasses livestock avoid to increase and grasses livestock favor to decrease26,27,28,29 (Figures 2 and 3; Figure S1; Table S4). We began with the concern that pikas compete with livestock for food and contribute to grazing-land damage. The evidence, however, points to a more complex relationship. Pikas choose what they eat, and their food does not necessarily overlap with livestock forage.30 They eat mainly grasses and sedges, but also many broad-leaved herbs, including legumes. In meadows dominated by *Elymus nutans*, a microscopic examination of stomach contents found that *Oxytropis* plants—including *O. glabra* and *O. kansuensis*—made up a substantial part of pika diets.31 These legumes contain alkaloids and other chemicals that usually deter plant-eating animals. Pikas appear able to deal with those chemicals through specialized microbes in their guts, helping them eat plants with the distinctive chemical makeup found in high-altitude grasslands.32

Pika diets also change with the seasons. In cold seasons they eat a wider variety of plants, including substantial amounts of *Potentilla anserina*, showing how they adjust their feeding as conditions change. When overgrazing allows plants that livestock find unappealing or avoid to spread, pikas tend to eat plants livestock do not prefer.3,33 Li and colleagues found that pikas can slow the spread of unwanted plants and help grasses and sedges favored by livestock grow.33 Thus, in well-managed pastures, pikas do not compete with livestock for food. Some competition may occur where grazing land is badly damaged and pika numbers are high, but pikas can still benefit livestock production.

We did not directly investigate pika diets in the field, which limits this study. Published research gives indirect evidence that pikas can vary what they eat, but without our own diet measurements we cannot explain the interactions between pikas and livestock in as much detail. We recommend using DNA metabarcoding—a method for identifying food from DNA traces—to measure pika diets across regions and seasons. That would provide stronger evidence for managing several animal species together in alpine grasslands.

### How grasslands changed over time under different measures

Overall, pika control and fencing did not substantially change the grasslands' characteristics (Figure 4). After pika control was put in place in 2011 and 2012, however, the amount of grasses livestock avoid increased significantly (Table S7). Pikas may hold back the growth of these grasses; reducing pika numbers could therefore have allowed more of them to grow.30

In grasslands that remained open to grazing (the Control), the number of kinds of grasses livestock favor and avoid, the total number of kinds of plants, and the amount of grasses livestock avoid all rose at first, then fell over time (Figure 4; Table S7). We mainly attribute this pattern to two linked effects of grazing. With enough light, other plants gradually filled spaces left by grazing, increasing the number of kinds of plants.34,35,36 Because livestock choose which plants to eat, grasses they avoid also moved into those spaces and increased in amount. Over time, as the grassland responded to grazing, the number of kinds of plants and grassland stability fell and eventually leveled off.

### Limitations of the study

Our monitoring network covered 14 years and 22 ecological regions, but several limits matter when interpreting the findings. First, although we covered a broad range of alpine meadows, most sites were in southeastern Qinghai Province. Northwestern Qinghai is largely uninhabited Gobi desert and barren land, without the grassland vegetation needed for grazing or monitoring. The patterns of change we identified may therefore not apply directly to those drier, sparsely vegetated areas or to other distinct high-altitude ecosystems. Second, we did not collect site-specific field data on what pikas ate. Published research and ecological indicators support our conclusions, but without detailed diet measurements—for example, from DNA metabarcoding—we cannot examine interactions between pikas and livestock as closely. Finally, we did not measure how differences in local social and economic conditions, or how closely communities followed the policies, affected their implementation. These differences could add complexity to the ecological outcomes we observed.

parts.abstract:
Summary

Controlling plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae) and fencing land to keep livestock out are two main ways people try to stop grasslands from worsening on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We studied 14 years of monitoring data from 1,460 plots in 22 ecological regions to assess these actions. A statistical model that examined linked relationships showed that reducing pika numbers had a small indirect negative effect on grassland stability. Long-term pika control and fencing did not produce important overall improvements. Under some grazing patterns, the number of plant species in both livestock-preferred and non-preferred grasses first rose by 18.7%, and the amount of non-preferred plant material rose by 27.4%. However, these gains faded after 8–10 years and returned to their starting levels. Our findings show that broadly controlling plateau pikas can reduce habitat quality without providing lasting benefits, while fencing large areas does not significantly improve grassland plant richness or stability. These results suggest that relying on one action at a time is not the best approach, and that management should be more joined-up and able to adapt to local ecology.

Subject areas: environmental science, environmental management, agricultural science
parts.introduction_first:
Making environmental policy can create a basic tension between science and practical decision-making. Science works by carefully building evidence, while policy-makers often need workable answers quickly.1,2 This clash is especially clear in ecosystem management, where complicated links and feedbacks in nature3 meet social and economic pressure for immediate solutions.1

China’s huge grazing landscapes, covering 4 million km2, show this challenge clearly. Since 2000, grassland restoration has mainly relied on long-term fencing, used for more than 25 years, and large plateau pika control programs for Ochotona curzoniae.4,5 These actions have received major investment—more than 12 billion since 2010—and cover 78% of degraded grasslands. Yet scientists still debate whether they make ecological sense and can work in the long term.6,7,8,9,10 New evidence points to unexpected results, including disrupted food-web effects3 and landscapes becoming more alike across space,4 which challenges the basic ideas behind today’s management approach.
parts.introduction_rest:
People have often treated plateau pikas as pasture pests because they are thought to compete with livestock for forage.3,11,12,13 This view has led to large control programs. In Mongolia, controlling Brandt’s vole costs US$300,000–800,000 each year.1,14 In China, large-scale rodent control began in the 1960s. The poisons used have included zinc phosphide, NH4+–fluoroacetate, and, more recently, anticoagulants such as diphacinone-Na and botulin toxin C.15 The Chinese Ministry of Agriculture reported that 38,000 tons of rodenticide were used each year from 2003 to 2005.3,16

But ecological research now shows a more complicated picture. By digging burrows, pikas act as ecosystem engineers: they help air move through the soil and help nutrients cycle through it.17 Their selective feeding may also reduce plants that livestock do not prefer and, under some conditions, support the growth of grass-like plants.18 This complexity means pika management needs to be reconsidered.

Fencing to keep livestock out remains a common way to restore degraded pasture because it is relatively affordable and can be used over large areas.8,19 Since 2003, China’s program to return grazing land to grassland has fenced 57,600 km2 of degraded alpine grassland in northern Tibet to exclude livestock.20 In 2011, a subsidy program expanded this effort by paying herders 90 RMB per hectare each year (12 USD per hectare each year) to fence degraded pastures.5 However, the ecological benefits of this fencing have not been fully assessed.3,5,8

Important questions also remain about whether today’s grassland actions can work across large areas and keep working over time. Many small-scale studies exist, but studies covering several ecological regions and longer periods are still rare.9,10

To address these questions, we set up long-term monitoring across 22 ecological regions, representing 85% of China’s alpine meadow biome, over 14 yearly surveys from 2005 to 2018. We monitored 1,460 randomly chosen plots, selected to represent different conditions, with an average of 66.3 plots in each region. We asked three main questions: (1) how does large-scale fencing to keep livestock out change the path of vegetation recovery and the benefits that grasslands provide; (2) does continued reducing of plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae) numbers create lasting changes in feeding relationships, or only move the visible problem elsewhere; and (3) after how long does the effectiveness of management begin to fade in grasslands that are still changing rather than settled into a stable state?

### Experimental model and study participant details

We studied the plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae), a small mammal found only on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We did not examine whether sex changed the results because management actions, including reducing pika numbers, were carried out across whole populations within specific ecological regions. We measured ecological responses at the scale of plant communities. All field observations involving animals followed institutional permissions and animal-welfare oversight.

### Method details

#### Study site

Our study took place in Qinghai Province on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Figure 1). This is a high-altitude region, usually 3,000–5,000 m above sea level.41,42 It has a harsh continental climate. The historical mean annual temperature was 0°C, and it was −0.5°C during the 2005–2018 study period. Average annual rainfall was 540 mm, with 70% falling from June to August (Figure 1).

The main soils were alpine meadow, scrub meadow, and bog soils.43 They support alpine meadows, shrublands, and steppes. Common plants include Carex species, Kobresia species, Stipa species, Achantherum splendens, and Potentilla fruticose.44

#### Experimental design

We compared three common management approaches: winter and summer grazing pastures (control), long-term fencing to keep livestock out (fencing), and reducing pika numbers (Figure 1). In May 2005, we set up 62 study areas across several counties in Qinghai. Each area covered more than 20 hectares and measured 500 m × 400 m. Management actions were kept in place through repeated periods lasting more than 3 years (Table S1). The sites represented the rolling land and sparse plant cover typical of grazed alpine pastures.

We set grazing levels using the Chinese agricultural industry standard NY/T 635-2015 for grassland carrying capacity. At all sites, grassland use was kept at about 1.0 yak per hectare, with a feeding rate of 45%–55%, following guidance from local grassland stations. In fenced areas, we installed permanent wire-mesh fences more than 15 cm above the ground. These kept out large plant-eating animals while allowing small animals, such as microtine rodents, to pass through.

We selected 30 pika-management sites where pika control had not been used before (Table S1). We reduced pika numbers in surrounding buffer zones larger than 20 hectares. Inside each zone, we marked a central measurement area smaller than 5 hectares. We controlled pika populations by placing wheat bait containing botulin C directly in pika burrows.

#### Field survey

In every study area, we set up five randomly placed 10 m × 10 m plots, at least 50 m apart. Each plot was more than 20 m inside the habitat boundary so that conditions near the edge would not affect the measurements. In each plot, we randomly placed three parallel 1 m × 1 m squares for plant sampling (Table S2).

We grouped plants as livestock-preferred grasses, non-preferred grasses, or avoidance grasses according to the feeding preferences of local livestock, especially yaks. We made these groups using regional plant guides and interviews with local herders about yak feeding behavior.45,46 For each 10 m × 10 m plot, we calculated plant-community measurements as the average of its three smaller sampling squares.

For each sampling square, we cut all plants at ground level. We dried the plants in an oven at 65°C for 48 hours, until their mass no longer changed. We then weighed the dry plant material on a balance accurate to 0.1 g. We monitored the sites every year in late July, when plant growth reaches its seasonal peak. This allowed us to compare the amount of standing plant material fairly across survey years.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Grassland index calculation

We defined the number of plant species as the total number of species found in each 1 m × 1 m sampling square. We described grassland stability using the inverse coefficient of variation (ICV),47 which compares average above-ground plant material with how much it varied over time:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here, μ is the average above-ground biomass across the experimental years. σ is the standard deviation, or the amount that above-ground biomass changed over time.

#### Statistical analysis

We carried out statistical analyses in R version 4.3.0. We used linear mixed-effects models with the `lmer` function in the `lme4` package, version 1.1.33. These models let us estimate how climate and management related to plant richness, grassland stability, and biomass in the three plant groups: avoidance, non-preferred, and livestock-preferred grasses.

In these models, management approach (control, fencing, or reducing pika numbers), climate conditions (mean annual temperature and annual rainfall), and combinations of these factors were treated as factors whose effects we estimated. County was included as a factor to account for differences among counties. Across all models, the total sample was 1,460 observations: all yearly measurements from study plots over the experimental period. In results from these models, three asterisks (***) indicate statistical significance at p < 0.05. This means that, if there were truly no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time. Summary graphs show averages ± SEM, a measure of how precisely we estimated the average. Graphs of change over time show 95% confidence intervals.

We used a statistical model of linked relationships, structural equation modeling (SEM), with the `psem` function in the `piecewiseSEM` package, version 2.3.0, to examine the processes linked to changes in grassland stability. We prepared the data using the `dplyr` package, version 1.1.2.48 We created most figures using BioRender.com.

## Results

### How restoration actions affected grasslands

Reducing pika numbers clearly increased the number of plant species overall, including livestock-preferred and avoidance plants, compared with the grazing control (p < 0.05). The estimated effects were 1.56–1.92 times those in the control areas (Figures 1 and 2). In contrast, fencing to keep livestock out did not show differences from the control areas in the number of plant species in any of the four groups: all plants, avoidance plants, non-preferred plants, and livestock-preferred plants. Fencing also did not change grassland stability or aboveground biomass—the plant material growing above the soil surface—for any of these four groups compared with the control. Reducing pika numbers did, however, increase aboveground biomass of avoidance plants, with an estimated effect of 1.85 (Figure 2).

**Figure 1. Geographic location and environmental conditions of the study sites in Qinghai Province**

(A) Boxplots show mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation at the study sites from 2005 to 2018. Boxes show the middle value and the middle half of values, while whiskers extend to 1.5 times that range.

(B) Maps show where the study plots were located across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

(C) Field photographs show the three management treatments: grazing (control), reducing pika numbers (PC), and fencing to keep livestock out.

**Figure 2. Effects of restoration actions on plant richness, stability, and aboveground biomass**

Values are means ± standard error of the mean (n = 1,460 observations). PC means reducing pika numbers; fence means fencing to keep livestock out. Three asterisks (***) mark results that were statistically significant at p < 0.05 in linear mixed-effects models. This means that, if there were truly no difference, a gap this large would occur by chance less than 5% of the time. Images were created using BioRender.com.

We also examined how plant communities responded in two representative plots. In the fenced plot, Banma96, grass-like plants such as *Poa annua* and *Elymas nutons* were dominant (Table S1). From year to year, the number of plant species and biomass in every palatability group remained stable (Figure S2).

In the plot where pika numbers were reduced, Gande85, avoidance plants made up 6.25%–23.53% of the whole plant community. *Oxytropis ochrocephala* Bunge was the dominant avoidance species. In this plot, both the number of avoidance plant species and their biomass increased significantly over time (Figure S2). Total plant-species abundance increased by 31.25% in the pika-controlled plot, compared with 6.25% in the fenced plot (Table S3).

Across the region, long-term fencing kept overall grassland conditions similar to those in the grazing control areas (Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). However, closer examination showed that responses differed among sites. Of 32 sites, total biomass increased significantly with fencing at 14 sites (p < 0.05), but decreased significantly at 18 sites (p < 0.05). The number of grass species increased significantly at 13 sites (p < 0.05) and decreased significantly at 19 sites (p < 0.05). Stability did not differ from the controls at any site (p > 0.05) (Table S6). These findings indicate that long-term fencing had little effect on grasslands at a broad scale, but its effects were mixed at smaller scales.

### Indirect effects of reducing pika numbers on grassland stability

Higher grassland stability was strongly associated with lower avoidance-plant biomass (−0.23) and higher non-preferred plant richness (−0.20) (Figure 3). Reducing pika numbers had an indirect negative effect on grassland stability. This mainly happened because changing resources affected the richness of avoidance plants, which then affected avoidance-plant biomass and finally reduced grassland stability.

Our statistical model of linked relationships fit the data statistically significantly for explaining grassland stability (p = 0.29). The model explained 13% of the variation in grassland stability.

**Figure 3. A statistical model of linked relationships showing the effects of reducing pika numbers in experimental grasslands**

All arrows show significant pathways. Numbers on the arrows are standardized regression coefficients, shown as “r” values. The mathematical signs show positive, negative, or two-directional relationships (±) (p = 0.29). Path diagrams were created using BioRender.com.

### How grasslands changed over time under different actions

From 2005 to 2018, fencing had little effect on plant richness or grassland stability (p > 0.05). In contrast, reducing pika numbers significantly increased the biomass of livestock-preferred grasses (p < 0.05). It also increased avoidance-plant biomass in 2011 and 2012 (p < 0.05). Overall, grasslands under both fencing and pika control rose and fell over time (Figure 4; Table S7).

**Figure 4. Changes over time in plant diversity and biomass under three management actions, 2005–2018**

The figure shows all plants, avoidance plants, non-preferred plants, and livestock-preferred plants under grazing (control), fencing, and reducing pika numbers (PC). Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals.

In the grazing control areas, total plant richness, livestock-preferred plant richness, non-preferred plant richness, and avoidance-plant biomass increased significantly during the 14-year period from 2005 to 2018. These increases were followed by significant declines, but the overall trend was still upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

### Grazing compared with fencing to keep livestock out

Our findings show that, across the region, long-term fencing to keep livestock out maintained grassland conditions similar to those under unmanaged grazing. At individual sites, however, the two approaches produced different results. This difference across scales challenges the common practice of using small fencing studies to predict what will happen across larger management areas.

Results also differed from site to site. Nearly half of the sites had more plant material after fencing, while others had less (Table S6). This pattern shows why one uniform management plan may not work in landscapes that vary greatly from place to place. Fencing did not produce one consistently positive or negative outcome. Instead, its effects appear to depend on local conditions, including the types of plants present, soil properties, and past grazing.

Generalizing from small fencing experiments may therefore lead to inaccurate predictions,21,22 because small studies often do not include enough of the environmental setting needed to judge management actions realistically.23 We recommend that future assessments use sampling designs at several scales so they can account for differences across the landscape. This would give more reliable guidance for targeted conservation strategies that fit the natural variation in grassland ecosystems.

Our monitoring network was mainly located in southeastern Qinghai Province. Northwestern Qinghai is mostly uninhabited Gobi Desert, with little or no grassland vegetation. It is not suitable for grazing, so we could not collect data there. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau also has major small-scale climate differences. Therefore, whether our conclusions apply to other regions needs further study. Research covering a wider geographic area would help test whether these patterns hold across different ecological and climate zones.

### Grazing compared with reducing pika numbers

Reducing pika numbers has been studied less often than fencing or grazing, but it is widely used in many places to protect livestock-preferred grasses. Unlike grazing, reducing pika numbers did not affect the amount of livestock-preferred grass. Instead, it led to a clear increase in both the number of avoidance-grass species and the amount of plant material they produced above ground (p < 0.05). A result with p < 0.05 is called statistically significant because, if there were truly no difference, a gap this large would occur by chance less than 5% of the time.

This pattern may result from complementary and selective effects. In other words, avoidance grasses may take over ecological spaces left open when livestock-preferred grasses have been reduced by long-term grazing under pika-control conditions.24,25 (Figure S1). However, as avoidance-grass biomass increased, overall grassland stability decreased (Figure 3). Reducing pika numbers on its own may therefore be inappropriate, because it could damage wildlife habitat while offering limited benefits for domestic livestock.

These findings challenge the usual view that plateau pikas increase avoidance grasses and reduce livestock-preferred grasses26,27,28,29 (see Figures 2 and 3; Figure S1; Table S4). This study began with the assumption that plateau pikas compete with livestock for food and worsen rangelands. But the evidence points to a more complex relationship. Plateau pikas choose what they eat, and their diet does not necessarily overlap with livestock forage.30

They mainly eat grasses and sedges, but also eat many broad-leaved herbs, including legumes. For example, microscope-based study of stomach contents found that Oxytropis species, including O. glabra and O. kansuensis, made up a substantial part of plateau pika diets in meadows dominated by Elymus nutans.31 These legumes contain alkaloids and other chemical compounds that usually discourage animals from eating them. Plateau pikas appear to cope with these compounds through specialized gut microbes, allowing them to eat plants with the distinct chemical makeup of high-altitude grasslands.32

Their diet also changes with the seasons, and they eat a greater variety of plants during cold seasons. Potentilla anserina is an important part of their diet then, showing how they adjust their feeding to environmental change. When overgrazing causes poorly palatable or avoidance grasses to spread, plateau pikas tend to eat plants that livestock do not prefer.3,33 Li et al. found that plateau pikas can slow the spread of undesirable plants and support the growth of grasses and sedges that livestock prefer.33 Therefore, in well-managed pastures, plateau pikas do not compete with livestock for food. In heavily degraded rangelands with many plateau pikas, some competition may occur, but plateau pikas can still benefit livestock production.

A limitation of our study is that we did not directly investigate plateau pika diets in the field. Existing research gives indirect evidence that their diet is flexible, but without our own field data, we cannot fully explain the mechanisms behind interactions between pikas and livestock. We recommend that future work use DNA metabarcoding, a method that identifies diet from DNA traces, to describe pika diets accurately across regions and seasons. This would provide a stronger scientific basis for managing several species together in alpine grasslands.

### How grasslands changed over time under different measures

Our findings show that reducing pika numbers and fencing to keep livestock out did not cause large changes in overall grassland characteristics (Figure 4). However, after pika-control measures were used in 2011 and 2012 (Table S7), avoidance-grass biomass increased significantly. This may be because plateau pikas can limit the growth of avoidance grasses,30 so these plants increased after pika numbers were reduced.

Under grazing conditions (Control), the number of livestock-preferred grass species, non-preferred grass species, and all grassland plant species, along with avoidance-grass biomass, first increased and then declined over time (Figure 4; Table S7). This pattern mainly reflects complementary and selective effects of grazing.

When enough light was available, plant species gradually filled ecological spaces opened by grazing pressure, increasing the number of plant species.34,35,36 Because livestock feed selectively, plants they avoid gradually occupied these open spaces, raising avoidance-grass biomass. Over time, the resilience of the grassland ecosystem caused grassland richness and stability to decline and eventually level off.

### Study limitations

Although our monitoring network covered a long period, 14 years, and a wide area, 22 ecological regions, several limits should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, while we studied many types of alpine meadow, our sites were mainly in southeastern Qinghai Province. This pattern largely reflects the northwestern region, which is mostly uninhabited Gobi Desert and barren land without the grassland vegetation needed for grazing or ecological monitoring. As a result, the patterns of grassland change over time that we identified may not apply directly to the drier, sparsely vegetated northwest or to other distinct high-altitude ecosystems.

Second, we did not collect direct, site-specific field data on plateau pika diets. Existing research and ecological indicators support our conclusions, but without detailed diet data, such as data from DNA metabarcoding, we cannot develop as detailed an understanding of interactions between pikas and livestock.

Finally, we did not directly measure how local social and economic conditions, or how closely communities followed these policies, affected the way the policies were put into practice. These factors could add further complexity to the ecological outcomes we observed.

Fencing to keep large grazing animals out remains a common way to restore damaged pastures because it is considered cost-effective and easy to expand.⁸˒¹⁹ China’s program to return grazing land to grassland, which began in 2003 and continues today, has fenced 57,600 km² of degraded alpine grassland in northern Tibet to keep livestock out.²⁰ In 2011, a subsidy program began paying herders 90 RMB/ha/year (12 USD/ha/year) to fence degraded pastures.⁵ But the ecological benefits of fencing have not been thoroughly evaluated.³˒⁵˒⁸

Important questions remain about whether grassland interventions can work across large areas and last over time. Many studies have examined small areas, but few have assessed multiple ecological regions over long periods.⁹˒¹⁰ To address these questions, we set up a monitoring network across 22 ecological regions, covering 85% of China’s alpine meadow biome, and followed it for 14 years, from 2005 to 2018. We monitored 1,460 plots selected to represent different parts of these regions, with an average of 66.3 plots in each region.

We asked three main questions: (1) How does fencing across large areas change the way grassland plants develop over time and the benefits grasslands provide? (2) Does long-term pika control lead to lasting changes in food-web relationships, or does it simply move the problem elsewhere? (3) How long do management benefits last before they begin to fade in grasslands that are continually changing?

### Experimental model and study participant details

We studied plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae), small mammals native to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. We did not analyze differences between males and females because management measures to control pikas were applied to whole populations within ecological regions, and we measured ecological responses across plant communities. All animal-related field observations followed institutional permissions and animal-welfare oversight.

### Method details

#### Study site

Qinghai Province lies on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Figure 1), where elevations are generally 3,000–5,000 meters above sea level.41,42 The region has a harsh continental climate. Its historical average annual temperature was 0°C and averaged −0.5°C during the study period, 2005–2018. Annual precipitation averages 540 mm, with 70% falling from June through August (Figure 1).

The main soil types are alpine meadow, scrub meadow, and bog.43 These soils support alpine meadow, shrubland, and steppe plant communities. Common plants include Carex spp., Kobresia spp., Stipa spp., Achantherum splendens, and Potentilla fruticosa.44

#### Experimental design

We compared three common management approaches: pastures grazed in both winter and summer (Control), long-term total fencing to keep large grazing animals out (Fence), and pika control (Figure 1). In May 2005, we established 62 study areas, each larger than 20 hectares (500 m × 400 m), across several counties in Qinghai. We kept the management measures in place in repeated cycles lasting more than three years (Table S1). The sites had the rolling land and sparse plant cover typical of grazed alpine pastures.

Grazing levels followed the Chinese agricultural industry code NY/T 635-2015 for carrying capacity. Across all sites, grassland use was set at about 1.0 yak per hectare, with a feeding rate of 45%–55%, based on guidance from local grassland stations. To keep large herbivores out, we installed permanent wire mesh fences more than 15 cm above the ground. This left openings for small animals such as microtine rodents.

We chose 30 pika management sites where no control had been used before (Table S1). Pika control was applied in surrounding buffer zones larger than 20 hectares. In each zone, we set aside a central sampling area smaller than 5 hectares for measurements. We carried out pika control by placing wheat bait containing botulin C directly in pika burrows.

#### Field survey

In each study area, we temporarily established five randomly placed plots, each measuring 10 m × 10 m. The plots were at least 50 m apart and more than 20 m from habitat boundaries, to avoid edge effects. Within each plot, we randomly placed three parallel 1 m × 1 m quadrats to sample plants (Table S2).

We grouped plant species as livestock-preferred plants, livestock non-preferred plants, or avoidance grasses based on what local livestock, especially yaks, eat. We used regional plant guides and interviews with local herders about yak feeding behavior to make these classifications.45,46 For each 10 m × 10 m plot, we calculated plant-community measurements by averaging the results from its three quadrats.

To measure plant biomass, we cut all vegetation at ground level in each quadrat. We dried the samples in an oven at 65°C for 48 hours, until their mass stopped changing, then weighed them on a precision balance that measured to the nearest 0.1 g. We monitored the sites each year in late July, when plants were at their seasonal growth peak, so that biomass could be compared consistently across survey years.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Grassland index calculation

We counted species richness as the total number of plant species in each 1 m × 1 m quadrat. We described grassland stability using the Inverse Coefficient of Variation (ICV),47 which compares average above-ground biomass over the study years with how much that biomass varied:

(Equation 1) ICV = μ/σ

Here, μ is the mean above-ground biomass across the experimental years, and σ is the standard deviation of above-ground biomass over time.

#### Statistical analysis

We carried out statistical analyses in R (version 4.3.0). We used linear mixed-effects models, which estimate relationships while accounting for differences among groups, with the ‘lmer’ function in the ‘lme4’ package (version 1.1.33). We measured how climate and management related to species richness, grassland stability, and biomass in three plant groups: avoidance grasses, livestock non-preferred plants, and livestock-preferred plants. Management (control, fencing, and pika control), climate (mean annual temperature and annual precipitation), and combinations of management and climate were included as factors that could explain the results. We also accounted for differences among counties in the model. Each model used 1,460 observations: all annual measurements from all study plots across the study period. In the linear mixed-effects model results, asterisks (∗∗∗) indicate statistical significance at p < 0.05. Summary plots show means ± SEM (standard error of the mean); plots of changes over time show 95% confidence intervals.

We used a statistical model of linked effects to examine the processes underlying changes in grassland stability. This structural equation modeling was run with the ‘psem’ function in the ‘piecewiseSEM’ package (version 2.3.0). We used the ‘dplyr’ package (version 1.1.2) to organize data, and created most figures with BioRender.com.
