## Results

### How the two methods affected the grasslands

We compared the fenced plots with the control plots, which were left un fenced. The plateau pika control made a clear difference to the number of plant species, both grasses that animals like to eat and grasses they avoid. It also made a clear difference to how much of the grassland the animals avoided (p < 0.05). The pika control raised the number of species by between 1.56 and 1.92 compared with the control (Figures 1 and 2).

The fenced plots, on the other hand, did not differ from the control plots in any of the four groups: all species, avoidance grasses, non-palatable grasses (grasses that animals do not like to eat) and palatable grasses (grasses that animals like to eat). In the same way, fencing did not change how stable the grasslands were, or how much plant material grew above the ground, for any of the four groups compared with the control. The pika control also had a positive effect on the weight of the grass that animals avoid (estimated effect = 1.85; Figure 2).

**Figure 1.** Where our study sites are in Qinghai Province and what the land is like

(A) Box plots show the average yearly temperature (MAT) and average yearly rainfall (MAP) at each study site from 2005 to 2018. Each box shows the middle half of the values (the interquartile range, or IQR), and the whiskers reach 1.5 times the IQR.

(B) Maps show where the study plots are spread across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

(C) Typical field photos show the three ways of managing the land: grazing (the control), plateau pika control (PC) and fencing (fence).

**Figure 2.** How the two methods affected the number of plant species, how stable the grasslands were, and the weight of the grass that animals avoid (AGB)

Values are averages ± standard error of the mean (SEM), a measure of how precisely each average is known (n = 1,460 observations). PC: plateau pika control; fence: fencing. Asterisks (∗∗∗) mark statistically significant results at p < 0.05, tested with linear mixed-effects models. Images were made with BioRender.com.

To see how the plants responded to each method, we looked at two typical plots. In the fenced plot (Banma96), most of the plants were grasses such as Poa annua and Elymas nutons (Table S1). In this plot, both the number of species and the weight of the plants stayed the same every year, for all four groups (Figure S2). In the plot under plateau pika control (Gande85), grasses that animals avoid made up between 6.25% and 23.53% of all the plants. The most common of these avoidance grasses was Oxytropis ochrocephala Bunge. This plot also showed a statistically significant rise in both the number of avoidance grass species and the weight of the grass that animals avoid (Figure S2). The pika-controlled plot had more species overall, by 31.25%, than the fenced plot, by 6.25% (Table S3).

Across the whole region, fencing for a long time kept the grasslands in much the same condition as the control (see Figure 2; Tables S4 and S5). When we looked at each site in turn, though, the results varied. At 14 of the 32 sites, the total weight of plants went up with fencing (p < 0.05), while at 18 sites it went down (p < 0.05). The number of grass species went up at 13 sites (p < 0.05) and went down at 19 (p < 0.05). How stable the grasslands were did not differ from the control at any site (p > 0.05) (Table S6). Taken together, these findings show that, over a large area, long-term fencing had very little effect on the grasslands, but its effects on the grasslands were patchy and uneven at smaller scales.

### The indirect effects of plateau pika control on how stable the grasslands were

We also used structural equation modeling to test a web of possible cause-and-effect links. We then checked how well these models matched the data. A model that matched the data well is called statistically significant.

The grasslands became more stable when the weight of the grass that animals avoided went down (−0.23) and the number of non-palatable grass species went up (−0.20) (Figure 3). In other words, keeping pika numbers down had an indirect harmful effect on how stable the grasslands were. This happened mainly through the way the pika control changed the number of species that animals avoid. That, in turn, changed the weight of the grass that animals avoid, and finally led to less stable grasslands.

The models also explained 13% of the differences in how stable the grasslands were. The models matched the data statistically significantly well (p = 0.29).

**Figure 3.** Structural equation models showing how well plateau pika control affected the grasslands, based on our experimental data

Every arrow is a statistically significant link. The numbers on the arrows are standardized regression coefficients (r values), which show how strong each link is on a common scale. The plus or minus sign (±) means a two-way link, or a link that goes in one direction and then comes back in the other. The p-value is 0.29. We drew the path diagrams with BioRender.com.

### How the grasslands changed over time under the different methods

Between 2005 and 2018, fencing had little effect on the number of grass species or on how stable the grasslands were (p > 0.05). The plateau pika control, however, made a statistically significant difference: the weight of the palatable grasses went up (p < 0.05). In 2011 and 2012, the pika control also increased the weight of the grass that animals avoid (p < 0.05). Overall, the grasslands under fencing and under the plateau pika control changed over time in a way that went up and down (Figure 4; Table S7).

**Figure 4.** How the number of species and the weight of different grasses changed over time under three methods (control, grazing; fence; PC, plateau pika control) from 2005 to 2018. All groups are all species, avoidance grasses, non-palatable grasses and palatable grasses.

Shaded areas show 95% confidence intervals, which are ranges that show how precisely each value is known.

Over the 14 years from 2005 to 2018, the control plots had a statistically significant rise in the total number of grass species, in the number of palatable grass species, in the number of non-palatable grass species, and in the weight of the grass that animals avoid. After that, this rose again, but then fell, so the overall trend was upward (Figure 4; Table S7).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

### Grazing versus fencing

Across the whole region, our results show that long-lasting fencing kept the grasslands in a condition similar to uncontrolled grazing. At the local level, though, the two methods led to very different results. This shows that a small-scale fencing study cannot simply be stretched to cover a whole, more varied landscape.

The results were not the same everywhere. Nearly half of the sites improved, while others declined. This shows that a single management plan does not work the same way everywhere on a patchwork of different landscapes (Table S6). Fencing did not always bring good or bad results. Instead, how well it worked seems to depend on local conditions, such as which plants grow there, what the soil is like, and how the land has been grazed in the past.

Fencing studies are often carried out in small plots. This common practice may lead to wrong predictions. Small studies often do not have the natural setting needed to judge properly how well a management method works. Instead, we recommend that future studies use sampling across many scales, from small plots to whole landscapes, so that they properly take account of how much the landscape varies. This would give more reliable guidance for conservation plans that fit the natural variety found in grasslands.

Our monitoring network was also spread mainly across southeastern Qinghai Province. The northwestern areas are mostly Gobi desert, a cold, dry region with no people living there. It has no grassland plants, so it is unsuitable for grazing and for monitoring. The climate on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau varies a great deal from one small patch of land to another. So it is still worth studying whether our conclusions apply to other regions. Future research covering a wider area would help check whether these patterns hold across different zones with their own climate and plants.

### Grazing versus pika control

Pika control is studied less often than fencing or grazing. Even so, it is widely used to protect grasses that animals like to eat in many places. Unlike grazing, pika control did not change the weight of the grass animals like to eat. Instead, it clearly improved the number of plant species and the weight of the grass that animals avoid (p < 0.05).

This can be explained by two effects that work together. First, the pika kept the grasses that animals like to eat from growing. Second, the pika made room for other plants. These are the grasses that animals avoid, which had been held back by grazing. The pika's presence filled these empty spaces.

However, the extra weight of the grass animals avoid made the grasslands less stable overall (Figure 3). So fencing on its own may not be a good idea. It could damage the places where wild animals live, even though it brings little benefit for farm animals.

These findings challenge the common belief that pika control makes more grasses animals like to eat and fewer grasses they avoid. The evidence suggests a more complicated picture. Pika animals choose where to look for food, and their diet does not necessarily clash with what farm animals eat. In fact, pika mainly eat grasses and sedges, but they also eat a lot of other flowering plants, including legumes such as clover and peas.

For example, scientists looked at the stomach contents of pika in meadows dominated by the grass Elymus nutans. They found that plants of the genus Oxytropis, including O. glabra and O. kansuensis, made up a large part of the pika's diet. These legumes contain alkaloids and other chemicals that usually keep plant-eating animals away. Pika seem to make up for these chemicals with special bacteria living in their gut, which lets them adjust their diet to the different plant chemicals found in high-mountain grasslands.

The pika's diet changes with the seasons, and they eat a wider variety of plants in the cold season. A plant called Potentilla anserina, a kind of grass, played a big part in this season. This shows that pika are adjusting their way of finding food as their surroundings change. In fact, when too much grazing makes grasses that animals avoid or do not like grow, pika tend to eat plants that farm animals do not prefer. Li and colleagues found that pika can slow the spread of unwanted plants and help grasses and sedges that farm animals like to grow. So in well-managed pastures, pika do not compete with farm animals for food. In badly damaged land where pika numbers are high, some competition may happen, but pika can still help farm animals.

Our study has a limitation: we did not study the pika's diet directly in the field. Bringing together earlier studies gives indirect evidence that pika can change their diet. But because we did not collect first-hand data, we cannot fully understand how pika and farm animals affect each other. We therefore recommend that future studies use a method called DNA metabarcoding. This method reads a short, standard stretch of DNA from each animal to work out what it has eaten. It would give a precise picture of what pika eat in different regions and seasons. That would give a stronger scientific basis for managing alpine grasslands with several species together.

### How the grasslands changed over time under different methods

Our results show that pika control and fencing did not cause large changes in the overall features of the grasslands (Figure 4). However, after pika control began in 2011 and 2012 (Table S7), the weight of the grass animals avoid rose significantly. This may be because pika can hold back the growth of these grasses. As a result, the weight of these plants went up once the pika population was reduced.

Under grazing (Control), the number of plant species, the number of grasses animals like to eat, the number of grasses they avoid, and the total weight of grasses first went up over time. After that, they went down (Figure 4; Table S7). This happened mainly because of the two effects described above.

The main reason is that grazing made room for other plants, and the pika then chose which ones to eat. When there was enough light, the plants that had been taken over by grazing slowly took their place. This led to more plant species. Because farm animals choose where to eat, the grasses they avoid gradually filled these empty spaces, and the weight of these grasses went up. Over time, the grassland became less able to recover. Its number of species and its stability fell, until they levelled off.

### Limitations of the study

Our monitoring network covered a long period (14 years) and many places (22 ecoregions). Even so, several built-in limits matter when reading our findings.

First, our study covers a wide range of alpine meadow types, but it was mostly focused on southeastern Qinghai Province. This is largely because the northwestern areas are mostly Gobi desert with no people living there, and bare land with no grassland plants. That is what makes it unsuitable for grazing and for monitoring. So the changes in plant life that we found may not carry over directly to these drier, sparsely vegetated northwestern areas, or to other high-mountain ecosystems.

Second, there is a clear gap in what we know about how pika and farm animals affect each other. We did not collect first-hand diet data for pika in the field. Earlier studies and ecological measurements give us a starting point for our conclusions. But because we did not measure the pika's diet in detail, for example with DNA metabarcoding, we cannot understand more precisely how pika and farm animals affect each other.

Finally, we did not directly measure how local social and economic conditions, and how well local communities followed the rules, affected the way these policies were carried out. This could have made the results even more complicated.
